paper_title: Instruction Capacity: Behavior and Degradation of Language Models under Controlled Load

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: The quality with which language models follow instructions falls as the load grows, yet there is still no quantity that expresses the limit of a model in units of load with an uncertainty. We propose an instrument in which the load consists of rules that replace single-token words in a text without meaning: such an instruction is atomic, the rules are independent by the construction of the task, and the outcome of every application of a rule is determined by a computable reference answer. Every occurrence of a word to be replaced becomes a Bernoulli trial with a known position in the answer and a known rule number. The statistical model first measures the shape of the dependence of the probability of a right replacement on the text length, the word position, the replacement density, the number of rules and the rule number, then describes it by smooth laws and restores a reference level that does not depend on the choice of the coding. The model yields the instruction capacity - the number of rules held at a given share of right replacements - with an uncertainty. A measurement of GPT-4o mini (2958 requests, 642,430 trials) gave regular laws for every load factor and for the collapse of the answer; the instruction capacity was about 37-38 rules at a share of right replacements of 0.95, and about 18-19 rules at the full replacement density. The code of the instrument, the measurement data and the passport are open, and every number of the passport is recomputed from the published points. The passport of a model serves as the calibration of a future meter of the instruction load of prompts.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Language models follow complex instructions, but this ability is limited. As the number of simultaneous conditions grows, model begins to lose some of them: it skips individual requirements, mixes up correspondences, and continues plausible text that no longer answers the statement of the task. The phenomenon is well known and has long been studied: the quality of execution falls with the number of instructions and with the length of the input and of the answer, and it depends on the place of an instruction in the prompt (Section 2). Yet there is still no quantity that would express the limit of model in units of load, carry an uncertainty and be measured in the same way for all models. The reason lies in the way the load is set. In existing works the instructions differ in nature and difficulty, share one coherent text or are checked by judge model, so the number of instructions is confounded with the composition of the set and with the growing difficulty of the task itself (Section 2.2). For the number of instructions to serve as measure of load, one needs an instruction that is atomic, independent of the others, homogeneous, checked by program, and that allows every application to be observed at its place in the answer. None of the approaches reviewed satisfies these requirements at once. 1 In the present work this instruction is rule that replaces one single-token word with another in text without meaning. rule admits exactly one right outcome at every place of its application, the rules are not linked to each other by the construction of the task, and the reference answer is computed by program. One rule becomes conventional unit of load, and every occurrence of word to be replaced becomes Bernoulli trial with known position in the answer and known number of the rule in the list. On these data we build statistical model that first measures the shape of the dependence of the probability of right replacement on every load axis and then describes it by smooth law. The model yields the instruction capacitythe number of rules model holds at given share of right replacementswith an uncertainty, and together with it the laws by which the quality of execution falls with every kind of load. The contributions of the work are as follows: an instrument with the simplest atomic instructionthe replacement of single-token word: task is generated from three seeds and reproduced byte for byte, the outcome of every trial is determined by computable reference answer, and the answer is checked line by line, distinguishing three kinds of failure (Section 3); statistical model without common level that depends on the choice of reference bins: the shape of the contributions of the axes is measured by bins and described by smooth laws, and an approximation shift correction restores reference level that does not depend on the coding (Sections 4.3 and 4.4); definition of the instruction capacity as the solution of an inverse problem, with an uncertainty computed by the delta method and with the spread of request difficulty taken into account (Section 4.5); the passport of GPT-4o mini: the laws of text length and word position, replacement density, number of rules and rule number (Section 5.3), the laws of the rate and the place of the collapse of the answer (Section 5.4), and the instruction, fatigue and guaranteed instruction capacities (Section 5.5); an open public part of the instrument from which every number of the passport is recomputed from the published points (Section 8). The value of the work is twofold. For the study of language model behavior it provides degradation laws with parameters and uncertainties that can be compared between models and between generations of models. For practice it lays the foundation of meter: the passport of model serves as calibration with which the instruction load of an arbitrary prompt can be expressed in the same units as the capacity of the model (Section 6). The paper is organized as follows. Section 2 describes the history of research on the behavior of language models under load and evaluates the approaches to measuring it. Section 3 describes the instrument, Section 4 the statistical model, and Section 5 the measurement and the passport of GPT-4o mini. Section 6 is devoted to perspectives, Section 7 sums up, and Section 8 describes access to the code and data.

sections.title: 2.1 History of research on language model behavior under controlled load
sections.content: The notion that the ability to hold and process information is limited, and that this limit can be measured, came from cognitive psychology. Miller [27] reduced experimental data to an estimate: in 2 short-term memory tasks person holds about seven meaningful unitsthe magical number seven, plus or minus two. Miller himself paid more attention to how grouping elements into meaningful units extends the memory span, and regarded the number seven rather as coincidence [4]. More than forty years later Cowan [4] brought together an extensive body of data and showed that the true limit is smaller: the central capacity of short-term memory is on average about four units, within the range from three to five. Thus the capacity of short-term memory became quantity that is measured, not only described. The second line, without which the very subject of this study would not exist, is the turning of instruction following into property of language model. Wei et al. [41] showed that instruction tuningfine-tuning model on set of tasks, each of which is described by an instruction in natural languagesharply improves zero-shot task solving: the 137-billion-parameter model FLAN, finetuned on more than 60 tasks, surpassed the 175-billion-parameter GPT-3 on unseen task types in 20 tasks out of 25. Ouyang et al. [34] fine-tuned GPT-3 on demonstrations of the desired behavior written by people, and then with reinforcement learning from human ratings. People preferred the answers of the resulting 1.3-billion-parameter model InstructGPT to the answers of the 175-billion-parameter GPT-3, although it has hundred times fewer parameters. Since then instruction following has been goal of training mass-market models, and how well model follows instructions has been subject of measurement. By 2023 the field had taken shape to the point of receiving its first detailed survey [25]: what an instruction is and what kinds there are, how to model instructions, on which datasets and with which metrics to test instruction following, and what affects it. The first systematic measurements answered the question of whether model follows given instruction. So that the check would depend neither on expensive and irreproducible human evaluation nor on biased evaluation by another model, Zhou et al. [45] proposed verifiable instructions requirements whose fulfilment is checked by program, for example write more than 400 words or mention the word AI at least three times. The IFEval set contains 25 types of such instructions and about 500 prompts, each with one or more instructions. Subsequent works began to increase the complexity. In FollowBench [22], at every level one constraint of one of five typescontent, situation, style, format, exampleis added to the initial instruction, from one to five constraints; for almost all of the 13 models studied the quality falls from the first level to the fifth, and the fulfilment of every constraint is evaluated by strong judge model. InFoBench [36] decomposes each of 500 instructions into simple criteria2250 yes/no questions in totaland counts the share fulfilled; the authors entrust the labeling of answers to GPT-4 as an accurate and cheap evaluator. ComplexBench [42] builds taxonomy of complex instructions4 types of constraints, 19 of their dimensions and 4 types of composition, that is, of the ways in which constraints are related to each other: simultaneously, in chain, by selection on condition, by nestingand derives the final score from the structure of the dependencies between the constraints; the check is performed by an evaluator model complemented by rules. In 2024 requirements began to be accumulated over the course of dialogue. In MMMT-IF [7] model answers questions about images in dialogue of up to 20 turns, and between the questions it receives requirements on the form of the answeron the length of the answer, on the first letter and the last character of sentence, on the length of sentence, on required word, on the parity of numberwhich stay in force until the end of the dialogue; up to six requirements are in force at once, and the fulfilment of each is checked by program. The share of fulfilled requirements, averaged over three models, falls from 0.81 at the first turn to 0.64 at the twentieth and decreases with the number of requirements in force: for Claude 3.5 Sonnet from one with one requirement to 0.74 with six, for Gemini 1.5 Pro from 0.68 to 0.4. If all requirements are repeated at the end of the input, the share of fulfilled requirements rises by 22.3 points on average: the difficulty lies not 3 only in fulfilling the requirements but also in finding them scattered over the dialogue. Multi-IF [17] stretches IFEval over three turns: at the second and the third turn one requirement is added, and the earlier ones remain in force; the set contains 4501 dialogues in eight languages. For all 14 models studied the fulfilment falls with every turnfor o1-preview from 0.877 to 0.707the models increasingly forget requirements that they fulfilled at earlier turns, and they make more errors in Hindi, Russian and Chinese. By the end of 2024 the evaluation of language models came to be regarded as an experiment with all its statistical requirements. Miller [26] showed that when questions are related to each otherfor example, several questions about one textthe standard errors must be computed with correction for this relation, and on real datasets they turn out to be up to three times larger than the naive ones (3.05 on DROP). In parallel ran yet another linethe limits of how model uses long input. Liu et al. [24] showed on questions over set of documents and on key-value retrieval that the accuracy depends on where in the input the needed item stands: it is highest when the needed item is at the very beginning or at the very end, and it drops noticeably when it is in the middle, even for models built for long context. RULER [20] extended the simple needle in haystack probe with multiple needles, multi-hop tracing and aggregation: almost all of the 17 models find single needle flawlessly, but the quality drops sharply with length, and although all of them claim window of at least 32 thousand tokens, only half hold satisfactory quality at this length. NoLiMa [29] removed the lexical overlap between the question and the needle, so that the needle can be found only through semantic link: 13 models with claimed window of at least 128 thousand tokens work well on inputs shorter than thousand tokens, but at 32 thousand the accuracy of 11 of them falls below half of their own accuracy on short input; even for GPT-4ofrom 99.3 to 69.7%. At the same time researchers carried the notion of working memory over from psychology to models. Gong et al. [11] gave ChatGPT (gpt-3.5-turbo) the n-back taska standard measure of human working memory in which, for every element of stream, one has to say whether it coincides with the element steps backand found in the model capacity limit strikingly similar to the human one; changing the wording of the instruction did not remove this limit, and the authors proposed n-back as reference probe of the working memory of language models. Gong and Zhang [10], training small transformers from scratch on this task, found that the total entropy of the attention weight matrix grows with n, and linked the limit to the dispersion of attention. Wang and Sun [40] carried over from psychology another classic technique as wellproactive interference, that is, interference from what was learned earlier. model reads stream of updates of keyvalue pairs and must name the last value of every key. The accuracy falls approximately log-linearly with the number of interfering updatesfor all models studiedand this regularity does not reduce to the length of the input: at fixed length, growing number of tracked keys gives the same decline (llama4-maverickalmost 100% on two keys and below 5% on 46), and in regression across models the model size is significant, but not the length of its context window. When prompt contains several instructions, it turned out that their order matters as well. Li et al. [23] asked models to write text with given required wordsfrom 3 to 20 words, 100 sets for each number, with permutations of the words and 20 repetitionsand found that the quality falls sharply as the number of constraints grows, and that fulfilment depends on the place of the word in the list for all models. The sign of this bias depends on the model: GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and LLaMA2-13b fulfil the early words of the list more often, LLaMA2-7b and LLaMA3-8b the late ones. Zeng et al. [44], permuting the constraints of one instruction and measuring how close the order is to hard-to-easy ordering, found that models of different architectures and sizes perform better precisely with this order, and linked this to how model distributes attention among the constraints. 4 Jaroslawicz et al. [21] measured the same phenomenon with large number of instructions: the ratio of the error share in the last third of the list to the error share in the first third. With few instructions it is close to one, at 150200 instructions it reaches peaklate instructions are violated noticeably more often than early onesand at extreme densities it levels out again: the errors are spread evenly over the list. Works on long context measured how model uses long input. LongGenBench [43] asked different question: does model keep following instructions while it itself writes long text. The prompt sets requirements on particular places of the future answer of 16 or 32 thousand tokens, and it is checked whether the requirement relating to each place of the answer is fulfilled there. Fulfilment falls as the answer grows longer: the deviation from the instructions is noticeable after 4 thousand tokens and grows towards 16 thousand. Requirements on places are fulfilled rarely: Qwen2-72B at length of 16 thousand tokens fulfils 24.0% of them. On the transition to 32 thousand the models moreover more often fail to finish the answer: Qwen2-72B writes 66.2% of the prescribed parts against 94.3%. Around 45% of the long answers degenerated into repetitions. In 2025 the number of simultaneous instructions became an independent load axis. IFScale [21] gives model from 10 to 500 instructions of one kindinclude given word in business report and measures the share fulfilled. Of 20 models, even the best fulfil only 68% at 500 instructions. The authors distinguish three forms of decline: threshold, when model is almost flawless up to critical density and then quickly loses quality and becomes unstable (the reasoning models o3 and gemini-2.5-pro), linear (gpt-4.1, claude-sonnet-4) and exponential (gpt-4o, llama-4-scout); at high density the errors are mostly omissions of instructions. Harada et al. [15] gave models up to ten instructions from IFEval at once and showed that the share of answers in which all instructions are fulfilled falls steadily with their number. logistic regression with single featurethe number of instructionspredicts this share with an error of about 10%, including for combinations of instructions that were absent from the training data. The same work shows that evaluation by judge model inflates the result: with ten instructions, 0.657 against 0.213 by the programmatic check. Load by many instructions was also studied on material from practice. AgentIF [35] takes the instructions of real agent applicationsthe system prompt of an agent together with user request. Unlike the short synthetic instructions of earlier sets, such an instruction is long and contains many constraints of different nature: on the form of the answer, on its content and style, on compliance with tool descriptions, and conditional ones (if . . . , then . . . ). Even the best of the models studied fully fulfils fewer than 30% of such instructions; models cope worst with complex structure of constraints and with tool descriptions. RECAST [14] starts from the observation that models stop coping when there are more than ten explicit requirements, while existing datasets contain no more than ten per example; the authors build training data with much larger number of constraints extracted from real prompts and show that fine-tuning on them improves the following of complex instructions. AdvancedIF [18] collects 1645 expert-written dialogues of three kinds complex instructions in single turn, requirements carried over many turns, and requirements of the system promptwith rubric of up to 20 criteria for each; the fulfilment of every criterion is evaluated by judge model, and an answer counts only if all of them are fulfilled. The best of the models studied pass about three quarters of the dialogues (GPT-5 in reasoning mode77.9% on average over the three kinds), and reinforcement learning in which the reward is the fulfilment of the whole rubric raises the result of Llama 4 Maverick by 6.7 points. At the same time it became clear that the measurements themselves are fragile. Dong et al. [5] test robustness: one and the same task is presented in several close variantsparaphrased, with restructured constraint, with distracting additionand model is credited with the task only if it solves all the variants. By this measure the quality turns out noticeably lower than by the usual 5 evaluation on IFEval: the drop reaches 61.8% of the original, and even for the most robust model, GPT-5, it is 18.3%. In 2026 load began to be set not only by the number of instructions. Mittal [28] loads model with parallel task: requirements on the form of the answer from IFEval are combined with tasks of growing difficultyfrom answering question to chain of arithmetic problems and the retelling of long text. Under this load the fulfilment of form requirements falls by 221%; requirements that must be fulfilled at the end of the answer suffer most (up to 50%), while prohibitions hardly suffer. The influence is mutual: form requirement can bring down the solution of the task itselffor one model the accuracy on the GSM8K arithmetic problems fell from 93 to 27%. As requirements accumulate, their joint fulfilment falls sharply, while repeating the instruction at the end of the prompt in many cases brings it back to 90100%. The check in all experiments is programmatic. SEQUOR [3] stretches the load in time further: constraints taken from real conversationson style, language, format, numerical limitsmust be observed over dialogue of 50 turns; compliance is evaluated by judge model. Even single constraint is observed worse and worse as the conversation grows longerfrom the first turn to the last the accuracy falls by more than 11%; with several constraints at once, by more than 38%; with their sequential introduction, by more than 40%. Replacing constraint in the middle of conversation restores the initial level, but then the decline is faster. in Eliav [6] tested whether the fulfilment of many rules depends on how they are presented: what format to write the rule list and where to place itin the system prompt or in the user message. The number of rules checked by program varied from 10 to 160. The number of rules itself proved decisive: by 80 rules the share of answers without single violation falls practically to zero for all five models, however the rules are presented. The way of presentation has weaker effect: the place of the rules matters no less than the format, but in different directions for different models, and there is no universally best format. Within few years the behavior of language model under load has turned from separate observations into subject of systematic measurement. It has been established that the quality of instruction following falls with the number of instructions, with the length of the input and with the length of the answer, depends on the place of an instruction in the list and on the order of instructions, falls under parallel task and over the course of dialogue, and that the working memory of models has limit similar to the human one. These results were obtained in different ways. The load was set by the number of instructions, their complexity, the text length, parallel task, the duration of dialogue; fulfilment was checked by program or by judge model; the result was expressed by the share of fulfilled instructions, the share of answers without violations or the shape of the decline curve. How suitable these ways are for measuring load is examined in the next subsection.

sections.title: 2.2 Evaluation of the testing methodology
sections.content: The works described above measure one and the same phenomenonthe decline in quality with growing loadbut in very different ways. To compare them, one must first say what we expect from measurement of load. We proceed from requirement on the meter: the load is set by the experimenter, the number of instructions serves as its measure, and the result is number with an uncertainty in units of this load. Nine criteria follow from this requirement. 1. Atomicity: every application of an instruction is Bernoulli trial: the outcome is binary and uniquely determined, there is no partial fulfilment, and the instruction does not decompose into sub-requirements that can be fulfilled separately. 6 2. Independence: the requirements of the instructions are separableeach instruction determines the correctness only of its own part of the answer, these parts do not overlap, and the set of correct answers is the product of the sets admissible for each instruction. Then the growth of the load is not confounded with the growth of the difficulty of the task, and the decline in quality is attributed to the model. The criterion does not require statistical independence of the outcomes: their dependence, arising in the model, is precisely the subject of measurement. This is the main criterion. 3. Homogeneity: at equal load the outcomes of different instructions belong to one distribution, that is, the instructions are exchangeable and the semantics of an instruction is not factor of the outcome. 4. Computable check: the reference answer is deterministic function of the task, and the outcome of trial is determined by an algorithm, without an evaluator. The error and the bias of the evaluation are zero, and the spread of the outcome belongs to the model alone. 5. Absence of extraneous factors: the outcome does not depend on quantities other than the measured oneunderstanding of the text, knowledge of the world, the wording of the instruction; the task is free of variance unrelated to the measured load. 6. Resolution by place: the unit of observation is single application of an instruction; for every trial the outcome and its covariates are knownthe position in the answer and the number of the instruction in the listso that the dependence of the success probability on the place is estimated, not averaged. 7. Scale: the region in which the experimenter sets the load (the number of instructions, the text length); it must cover the transition of the success probability from close to one to small, otherwise the parameters of the dependence are not identifiable and the capacity is obtained by extrapolation. 8. Precision: when the measurement is repeatedunder the same conditions or by an independent experimenter on new random sample of tasksthe results agree within the stated uncertainty; for this the procedure is fully specified: the generation of tasks, the model version, the generation parameters, the reference answer and the processing. 9. Protection against memorization: tasks are generated at random for every measurement and cannot coincide with the training data of the model, so the right outcome cannot be obtained by reproducing something memorized. Two of these criteriathe computable check and the absence of extraneous factorscoincide with what the practice of evaluating AI agents advises [12]: to check by program wherever possible and by judge model only where it cannot be avoided, and to start every trial from clean state, because state shared by trials makes their outcomes dependent for reason that has nothing to do with the model under test. By the way the load is set, the works of Section 2.1 fall into five approaches: form instructions checked by program; composite constraints checked by judge model; required words in coherent text; synthetic probes of memory and context; long answer with placed requirements. Below each approach is examined against these criteria, and the result is summarized in table at the end of the subsection. 7 Form instructions checked by program. Requirements on the form of the answer are added to substantive taskto write an essay, letter, program: length, number of paragraphs or sentences, required and forbidden words, letter case, punctuation, code style rules. The fulfilment of each requirement is checked by program, and the load is the number of requirements in one prompt. This is how IFEval [45], the ManyIFEval and StyleMBPP sets [15], the experiments with parallel task [28] and with up to 160 rules [6] are built, and in dialogue, where requirements accumulate over the turns, MMMT-IF [7] and Multi-IF [17]. The programmatic check is the main merit of the approach, but it serves as reference only approximately. The check here is heuristic over free text, not function of the task: the authors of IFEval found false rejections in it (a required phrase highlighted with markup is not recognized) and introduced second, loose check that transforms the answer before the comparison. The outcome of trial depends on which check is used. There is no independence, and this is the main point. All requirements apply to one and the same text: length, number of paragraphs, letter case and punctuation constrain the answer as whole, so every new requirement narrows the set of answers admissible for the others. The authors see this themselves. IFEval notes that simple combination of instructions yields contradictions no more than five paragraphs and fewer than 20 words; Harada et al. [15] compiled map of conflicts between 15 instructions (a limit on the number of characters against the number of paragraphs, upper case against lower case) and combined only compatible ones; Mittal [28] kept 11 types out of 15 for stacking requirements, excluding structural conflicts; in MMMT-IF mutually exclusive variants of requirement are gathered into one category, of which at most one is in force, and in Multi-IF contradicting requirements of different turns are filtered out by model and then by people. Selecting compatible requirements removes explicit contradictions but does not make the task separable: compatible requirements still share one text. The consequence is visible in the data: the rule no more than 79 characters per line alone is fulfilled in 97 and 99% of cases (Claude 3.5 Sonnet and Gemini 1.5 Pro), and together with five other code style rules in 2 and 20%. Which part of this decline falls on the limit of the model and which on the increased difficulty of the joint task cannot be established from such data. Atomicity is partial. Some requirements are checked by single feature of the whole answer length, number of paragraphs. Others are conjunction over the whole text: no commas, only lowercase letters, every line no longer than 79 characters decompose into sub-requirements on every sentence, word or line and are violated by one place out of many; one extra comma and twenty give the same outcome. There is no homogeneity: different requirements are fulfilled with different probabilities already in isolationfor GPT-4o from 0.62 (an exact number of characters) to 1.0 (a title, quotation marks, ban on commas), and Harada et al. [15] excluded instructions with very low success from the set in advance. Therefore the result depends on which requirements made it into the set, and the number of requirements is confounded with its composition. There are extraneous factors: form requirements are imposed on meaningful text on given topic, and the outcome changes noticeably when the same requirement is paraphrased [5]; in dialogue an image that must be understood (MMMT-IF) and the language (Multi-IF) are added to them. Resolution by place is partial: the unit of observation is requirement in the whole answer or the whole answer, and where in the answer requirement is violated is not recorded; in dialogue the outcome is known for every turn, that is, by place in time [7, 17]. Scaleup to 5 simultaneous requirements in Mittal [28], up to 6 in Epstein et al. [7], up to 10 in Harada et al. [15], up to 160 in Eliav [6]. In the experiments of Harada et al. [15] the probability of fulfilling single requirement remains high (for GPT-4o0.85 with ten requirements against 0.94 with one), and only the share of answers in which everything is fulfilled covers the transition (from 0.94 to 0.21). In Eliav [6] this share reaches practically zero already by 80 rules, and over 8 the second half of the range the measure distinguishes nothing. Precision is unattainable in this approach by construction: requirements differ in difficulty, so new sample of tasks gives different result because of different composition of the set, not because of the model. Only run on the same tasks can be repeatedas Harada et al. [15] did three times for one modelbut this is check of the repeatability of run, not of the measurement. There is no protection against memorization: IFEval was published in 2023 together with 541 prompts, derivative works take their tasks from it (Harada et al. [15]216 task descriptions, Mittal [28]the original prompts verbatim, He et al. [17]the first turn of every dialogue), and these tasks may end up in the training data of models released later. Thus the approach provides programmatic check and wide range of the number of requirements, but the number of requirements does not serve in it as measure of load: the requirements share one text, differ in difficulty, and as their number grows the task itself changes. Composite constraints checked by judge model. An instruction contains several substantive constraintson content, style, situation, format, example, on the use of toolsand the fulfilment of each is evaluated by judge model, and by rules where the answer is closed. The load is increased by adding constraints to the same instruction [22], by linking them with conditions and nesting [42], by stretching them over the time of dialogue [3], by taking long instructions from practice [35] or by entrusting their writing to experts [18]. The goal of these works is to bring the measurement closer to real use, and almost all the deviations from the criteria are the price of this goal. The difficulty begins already with atomicity: substantive constraint has no unique outcome. Whether an answer matches style, situation or given content is matter of judgment, and the experts who labeled answers for FollowBench agree with each other in only 85% of cases. InFoBench [36] decomposes an instruction into yes/no questions, but question about style or content remains judgment. If the right outcome is not uniquely defined, program cannot provide it; hence the judge model, and with it the error and the bias of the evaluation. They are large. The FollowBench judge agrees with the experts in 88% of cases, but without the description of how the constraints were added the agreement drops by 9 points, and with template of overall quality assessment to 67%: the result depends on how the request to the judge is worded. The SEQUOR judge wrongly rejects 11.5% of correct answersas much as the measured decline over 50 turns with one constraint (more than 11%), and the data do not allow checking whether the error of the judge itself grows with the length of the conversation. On form instructions, where programmatic check exists, the judge inflates the share of fully fulfilled answers threefold: 0.657 against 0.213 with ten instructions [15]. The AdvancedIF judge, the o3-mini model, agrees with the expert labels on individual criteria with an F1 measure of 0.723 [18]. Moreover, the judge is biased: in the MMMT-IF experiments GPT-4o as judge rates the answers of GPT-4o higher, and Gemini the answers of Gemini [7]. There is no independence, and its absence is built in deliberately. FollowBench obtains each next level of complexity by adding constraint to the same instruction. ComplexBench builds compositionsa chain, selection by condition, nestingthat is, dependencies between constraints; the authors themselves write that because of this coupling the constraints are hard to evaluate separately, and they assemble the final score from the structure of the dependencies. In SEQUOR and AgentIF all constraints act on one and the same conversation or answer of an agent. The growth of the number of constraints here is inseparable from the growth of the difficulty of the task: this is precisely the subject of study, but the number of constraints does not then serve as measure of load. 9 There is no homogeneity: constraints of different types differ in difficultyin AgentIF models cope worst with complex structure of constraints and with tool descriptions. Extraneous factors lie at the very core of the approach: substantive constraint cannot be fulfilled, nor its fulfilment evaluated, without understanding the text and knowing the world, and this is required both of the model under test and of the judge. Resolution by place is partial: InFoBench and ComplexBench give an outcome for every yes/no question, SEQUOR for every turn of dialogue, that is, by place in time; the position within the answer is not recorded. The scale is small, and in some of the works the load is not set by the experimenter: FollowBenchfrom one to five constraints, SEQUORup to three at once, in existing datasets, according to the survey of Guo et al. [14]no more than ten per example. AgentIF has on average 11.9 constraints, but their number is determined by real instruction, not by the experimenter, so the load region is not planned at all. Precision rests on the judge. The judge is part of the measuring instrument: the result depends on the choice of the judge model and on the template of the request to it, and the measurement can be repeated only while the same version of the judge is available. Added to this is the same as in the previous approach: the constraints differ in difficulty, and new sample of tasks gives different result because of different composition. There is no protection against memorization: the sets are fixed and published. The approach is closest of all to real use, but it pays for this with measurability: the outcome is not uniquely defined, the constraints are coupled by construction, and they are checked by model with its own error comparable with the measured effects. Required words in coherent text. model writes coherent text and must include given words in it; the load is the number of words. IFScale [21] gives from 10 to 500 business terms for business report; Li et al. [23] take sets of concepts from which plausible sentence must be composed, and sets of up to 20 required words. Fulfilment is the presence of the word in the answer, checked by program. This is the approach closest to ours. Atomicity holds: requirement is one word, the outcome is binary and unique. The presence of word is checked by program by exact match. But which answers enter the count is decided by model: IFScale repeats the request if the answer is plain list of words, refusal or, according to the o4-mini model, an incoherent report. The count is taken over the answers selected by the judge. There is no independence, and the reason is visible in the same rejection. Without the requirement of coherence the task is trivialto list the wordsand it is precisely such answers that IFScale discards. The difficulty is created by coherence, and coherence couples all the words: each must be fitted into one meaningful text together with all the others, and the difficulty of fitting in word depends on which words and how many of them must stand in the same text. The growth of the number of words is therefore confounded with the growth of the difficulty of the task. There is no homogeneity, and the authors of IFScale account for this themselves. For every word they estimated the difficulty of generating it by the perplexity of small model, selected the 500 hardest and chose words stratified by difficulty so that the runs would be comparable. Stratification is needed precisely because the result depends on which words came up. This difficulty is semantic: word must be fitted into business report, in Li et al. [23] into plausible scene, and success depends on how well the word suits the topic. For the same reason the extraneous factors cannot be removed: model writes meaningful text, and the outcome depends on the understanding of the topic and of the meaning of the words. Resolution by place is only by the number in the list: IFScale compares errors at the beginning 10 and at the end of the list, Li et al. [23] by the position of word in the prompt. Where word stands in the answer is not recorded: presence anywhere counts. The scale is the largest among the works found: from 10 to 500 words in steps of 10. And yet the transition is not covered for all models: in the words of the authors themselves, the strongest models do not yet collapse at 500 words. Precision is better attainable here than in the previous approaches: the tasks are generated by rule, and every measurement is repeated on five random samples of words. But the comparability of the repetitions has to be ensured by selecting the samples by word difficulty, so the result is defined only relative to the composition of the vocabulary. IFScale has protection against memorization: the set of words for every request is random, and there is no ready right answer that could be memorized; part of the experiments of Li et al. [23] is built on the published CommonGen set. The approach preserves atomicity and the computability of the check and brings the number of instructions to hundreds. But coherent text couples the words with each other, and the success of inserting word depends on its meaning, so the number of words measures not only the load but also the difficulty of placing them together. Synthetic probes of memory and context. model receives synthetic task with computable answer: to say whether letter coincides with the letter steps back [11, 10], to name the last value of key in stream of updates [40], to find value by key or an answer among documents [24], to find one or several needles in long text [20, 29]. There is one instruction, and it does not change; the load is the amount of information that must be held or found: the depth n, the number of updates and keys, the length of the input and the place of the needed item in it. The answer is short. By most criteria this is the strictest of the approaches. Every probe is one trial with unique answer, and the check is an exact match. Answers to different probes do not constrain each other: the value of each key and the coincidence of each letter are determined separately, and the difficulty comes from the input, that is, from the controlled load; the interference in PI-LLM is set in the input and serves precisely as such load, not as link between requirements on the answer. Homogeneity and the absence of extraneous factors are achieved by the authors deliberately: Liu et al. [24] make the keys and values random identifiers to remove the meaning of language as confounding factor, and Wang and Sun [40] pick words from the vocabulary at random in every run to exclude the influence of particular semantic combinations. There are two exceptions, and both are deliberate. NoLiMa requires finding the needle through semantic link that relies on In questions over documents knowledge of the worldmeaning is the subject of study here. model also answers from memory: without any documents GPT-3.5 answers correctly in 56.1% of casesbetter than when the needed document stands in the middle of the input [24]. Resolution by place exists, but by place in the input: the accuracy is measured as function of where the needed item stands. Place in the answer does not arise as question: the answer is short. The scale is large and covers the transition: an input of up to 128 thousand tokens in RULER and up to 32 thousand in NoLiMa, up to 400 updates per key and up to 46 keys in PI-LLM, where the accuracy of one model falls from almost 100 to less than 5%; the exception is n-back, where the depth reaches only three. Precision is attainable: the material is generated by rulerandom identifiers, words, letter sequencesand repetition on new sample is natural; Wang and Sun [40] give confidence intervals over multiple repetitions. For the same reason there is also protection against memorization. The authors of NoLiMa take special care of itthey assemble the haystack text from random short passages of open booksalthough the needles themselves are fixed set of 58 questionneedle 11 pairs; the questions over documents in Liu et al. [24] lack it. The approach is closest of all to the requirements of measurement, but it measures something else: holding and finding information in the input with short answer, not the simultaneous execution of many instructions. The number of instructions does not serve in it as the load, and how execution changes over the course of long answer is not observed. Long answer with placed requirements. LongGenBench [43] tests whether model fulfils requirements tied to particular places of long answer. The model writes text of parts of the same typea diary with an entry for every day or week of year, description of every floor of skyscraper, plan of city blocksand the prompt contains seven requirements, each of which names fact and the part of the answer where this fact must appear: for example, the wifes birthday in the entry for June 29. requirement may also apply to several consecutive parts or repeat with given step. The load is the length of the answer: the short variant of the task is designed for 16 thousand tokens, the long one for 32 thousand. Whether the required fact is in the right part is decided by the Llama 3.1-8B model. The strength of the approach is that the requirements are tied to places of the answer and the outcome of each is known where it must be fulfilled. The authors show how fulfilment changes over the course of the answer: it drops noticeably after 4 thousand tokens. True, this dependence is given only as smoothed curve, and the numbers in the tables are shares over all answers, so resolution by place is partial. Facts, dates and places are substituted into templates at random, so the tasks cannot end up in the training data of model. For the same reason precision is attainable: new sample of tasks is drawn from the same templates with the same composition of requirements; but the authors do not report the uncertainty. There is no independence, for the same reason as with required words: the requirements are facts that must be fitted into one coherent text. diary is the story of one person, and vacation, birthdays and regular activities must fit into it together with everything the main task requires: an entry for every day or week, the weather, work. range requirement occupies several consecutive parts, periodic one repeats over the whole answer, and the dates for all requirements are chosen at random, so the parts of different requirements may coincide. Every requirement is also linked to the main task: it can be fulfilled only in part that the model has written at all, and in the long variant the models more often fail to finish the answerQwen2-72B writes 94.3% of the prescribed parts at 16 thousand tokens and 66.2% at 32 thousand. There is no homogeneity, twice over. Requirements of the three kinds are built differently: requirement on one part is fulfilled if the fact is in it, while range or periodic requirement only if the fact is in every one of many parts; such requirements are harder than single ones and, moreover, not atomic. The facts themselves also differ: fitting birthday into diary and placing gym on the 34th floor of skyscraper are tasks of different difficulty, and, as with required words, success depends on how well the fact fits the text. Hence also the extraneous factors: fulfilment depends on the understanding of the topic and on how the model builds coherent text. And program cannot check such requirement: whether the fact is in fragment of free text is decided by the Llama 3.1-8B model, and although on 300 manually labeled cases it agreed with people in all of them, the reference remains its judgment. The scale is narrow. There are always seven requirements, so the approach does not allow loading model with the number of instructions; only the length serves as the load, and it has two values. These are, moreover, two different tasksa diary by weeks and by days, skyscraper of 100 floors and of 300so together with the length the number of parts and their content change, and the actual length is determined by the model, not by the experimenter. The approach places requirements on places of long answer and knows the outcome of each at its place. But the requirements in it are substantive facts of one coherent text, different in kind and meaning, they are checked by model, and the load is set by two different tasks. What these measurements provide. The result in the works reviewed is expressed in one of three ways. Most often it is the share of fulfilled instructions at the loads that the authors tested. Sometimes it is the share of answers in which all instructions are fulfilled. The shape of the decline, finally, is described in words: three forms in IFScale, an approximately log-linear decline in PI-LLM, knee in Eliav [6]. Some authors estimate the uncertainty by repetitions, others construct confidence intervals, as MMMT-IF does for the share of fulfilled requirements at every turn [7], and still others do not report it at all. For scientific research these data are valuable but insufficient. They show that the phenomenon exists: the quality of execution falls with the number of instructions, with the length of the input and of the answer, and depends on the place of an instruction. They do not allow studying it comprehensively. The load is tested at few points, and share obtained at chosen load depends on which points the experimenter chose and cannot be compared with the result of another work. Closest of all to describing the dependence itself came Harada et al. [15]: their logistic regression covers all the tested numbers of instructions, but the authors do not derive from it the load that model withstands with given reliability. Moreover, when outcomes are related to each other, like the outcomes of the instructions of one answer, the uncertainty must be computed with correction for this relation; without the correction the interval comes out narrower than the true one, on real datasets up to three times [26]. model maker needs parameter of the model: one number with an uncertainty, measured in the same way for all models, by which they can be compared with each other. Model makers already compare models by one number when it comes to compliance with given rules of behavior: OpenAI publishes for each model the share of answers that comply with the behavior specification of its modelsfrom 72% for GPT-4o to 89% for GPT-5 Thinking [13]. For load by instructions no work provides such parameter. IFScale makes it possible to rank models by the share fulfilled at 500 instructions, but this is single point, and the strongest models do not yet collapse at it. The regression of Harada et al. [15] contains no load parameter. For another phenomenonthe use of long inputsuch parameter already exists. RULER and NoLiMa define the effective length: the largest of the tested input lengths at which the quality of model stays above threshold. It can be compared between models; for GPT-4, for example, with claimed window of 128 thousand tokens it equals 64 thousand. This parameter is coarse: the tested lengths go in doublings, so it is known only to within factor of two, and it has no interval. Works on instruction following study the needed phenomenon and bring the tasks ever closer to real use: the instructions in them are substantive, linked by common text and increasingly checked by judge model. But the closer task is to real use, the less in it lends itself to measurement. Synthetic probes of memory and context, on the contrary, are built as measuring instrument: the outcome in them is unique, the tasks are generated at random, and the load is set by the experimenter. sections.title: 3 The Instrument
sections.content: To measure the degradation of language model under various kinds of load we built an instrument software system that generates tasks, presents them to model and checks its answers. By construction the instrument satisfies the criteria of Section 2.2: the load is set by the experimenter, the material of task is generated at random and carries no meaning, and the outcome of every application of an instruction is unique and checked by program. The load is formed by instructions that the model must execute simultaneously. task consists of text and list of instructions for it. The text is stream of words from fixed vocabulary of single-token nouns, without meaning and punctuation, broken into lines of ten words (Sections 3.2 and 3.3). An instruction is rule that replaces one word of the text with another word of the vocabulary (Section 3.1). The model must apply all the rules to the text, keeping it otherwise unchanged. task is determined by six numbers: the number of rules m; the number of distinct words of the text D; the number of repetitions of each word n; three seeds of the random number generatorthe rule seed, the text seed and the rule order seed (Section 3.3). 14 The answer of the model is compared with reference answer computed by program, and every occurrence of word to be replaced becomes trial with the outcome 1 or 0. For every trial the number of its rule in the list and the position of the word in the answer are known (Section 3.4). The result of measurement is the outcomes of the trials; the degradation of the model shows itself in decrease of the share of right replacements as the load grows (Section 3.5).

sections.title: 3.1 The atomic instruction—word replacement
sections.content: A rule is written as lake -> stone: the model must replace every occurrence of the word lake in the text with the word stone. Such rule is an atomic instruction. It applies to one word and does not decompose into simpler requirements, and at every place of application it admits exactly one right outcome: the word stone must stand in place of the word lake. These properties make rule suitable for measurement. The correctness of every application is established by comparison with the reference answer, without judgment about the quality of the answer. The rules are not linked to each other: each applies to its own word, and executing one does not change what is required to execute another. Therefore the load can be increased to hundreds of simultaneous rules without changing the nature of the task. Finally, executing rule does not depend on understanding the content of the text. Both words of rule are one token for each of the tokenizers compared, so rule maps one input token to one output token (Section 3.2). One rule serves as conventional unit of load, and the number of rules as the measure of load. The unit is conventional: it is defined by the protocol of the instrumentthe prompt template, the structure of the text and the rules of answer checkingand by the vocabulary. Values expressed in rules are comparable between models measured under the same protocol. The task requires of the model neither reasoning, nor knowledge of the world, nor arithmetic, nor understanding of the text. Therefore an error of the model reflects, with high probability, the limit on the number of independent correspondences that the model can hold and apply simultaneously, not misunderstanding of the task.

sections.title: 3.2 Construction of the vocabulary
sections.content: The text of task and the rules are composed exclusively of words of fixed vocabulary, and the composition of the vocabulary determines what exactly the instrument measures. The vocabulary serves three purposes: standardization of the material: tasks for all models are built from the same words, and the data obtained on different models are comparable with each other; reproducibility: task is built by random choice of words from fixed list and can therefore be restored from the seeds of the generator; interchangeability of words: one word differs from another only by its role in the task, not by its own properties, which would otherwise enter the measurement; the residual differences of particular words, including semantic ones, are smoothed out because every load is measured on different random sets of words and rules (Section 3.3). Four requirements on the words of the vocabulary follow from these purposes: word is encoded as one token by each of the tokenizers comparedthen replacement remains an atomic operation, partial replacement of word is impossible, and the length of the prompt in tokens does not depend on the choice of words; 15 word is monosyllabic nounthis ensures the homogeneity of the material, and replacing noun with noun preserves the grammar of the stream; word is in the singular, which excludes pairs such as arm/arms that would turn replacement into test of morphology; word is at least three letters long, which excludes the names of letters and function words. The initial list for the vocabulary consisted of all entries of the CMU Pronouncing Dictionary (cmudict.0.7a)123 455 words. The CMU Pronouncing Dictionary, like the WordNet database used further on, is distributed as fixed version, so rebuilding the vocabulary gives the same result. From the initial list we kept the words written only in lowercase Latin letters and at least three letters long. We determined the number of syllables from the phonetic transcription of word in the CMU Pronouncing Dictionary: in it every vowel phoneme is marked with stress digit, and the number of such phonemes equals the number of syllables. Monosyllabic words remained. We determined the part of speech and the number of word from the WordNet 3.0 database. The words that are nouns and coincide with their base form (lemma), that is, stand in the singular, remained. The last step was the single-token check. We encoded every remaining word, with space before it, with three tokenizers: o200k_base (the gpt-4o and gpt-4o-mini models), cl100k_base (gpt-3.5-turbo) and the tokenizer of the Qwen2.5 model. The space was added because in the text of task and in the rules word stands after space, and tokenizers encode the word together with it. The vocabulary includes the words that give exactly one token with all three tokenizers. Table 2 shows the number of words remaining after each step. Table 2: Selection of the words of the vocabulary v1_intersection: the number of words after each step. Step Entries of the CMU Pronouncing Dictionary Only lowercase Latin letters At least three letters One syllable WordNet nouns Singular: the word coincides with its lemma One token for each of the three tokenizers Words 123 455 115 533 115 318 14 884 5750 3581 2220 The current version of the vocabulary has 2220 words from three to eight letters long. This makes it possible to form tasks with up to 2048 words and more. The single-token property of the words of this version is guaranteed only for the three tokenizers listed. For model with different tokenizer the vocabulary is built anew by the same rules, and the single-token property is required only for the tokenizer of the model under study: common vocabulary for all models is not needed, because the comparability of measurements is ensured by averaging over random sets of words and rules. The vocabulary, together with the code for building and validating it, like the other materials, is published in the GitHub repository (Section 8).

sections.title: 3.3 Construction of a task
sections.content: The load of task is determined by three parameters: the number of rules m, the number of distinct words of the text and the number of repetitions of each word n. The triple (D, n, m) 16 is called point and sets the position of the task in the load space. The parameters are bounded by the conditions 1 and + 2220, which follow from the size of the vocabulary (Section 3.2). task is formed by rule list and text substituted into fixed prompt template. point determines only the load parameters; the specific material of task is determined by three seeds of the pseudorandom number generator: the rule seed sets the choice of the words of the rules and their division into pairs; the text seed sets the choice of the background words and the order of all words in the text; the order seed sets the order of the lines in the rule list. task at point, together with the answer of the model to it, is called request. In the published data of the instrument request corresponds to point record. Requests at one point with different seeds realize one and the same load on different material; averaging over them smooths out the residual differences related to particular words. The prompt is deterministic function of the point, the three seeds and the vocabulary and is reproduced byte for byte, so the task of every published request can be restored and checked. To build the rule list, the generator initialized with the rule seed chooses 2m words without replacement from the vocabulary sorted alphabetically. The first words become the words to be replaced, the last their replacements, and the pairs are formed in order. Sorting the vocabulary makes the result of the choice independent of the internal storage order of the words. The sets of words to be replaced and of replacements do not overlap, so the rules do not form chains such as lake -> stone, stone -> fish, and the execution of each rule does not depend on the others. The position of rule in the list, the rule number r, is recorded for every trial. With zero order seed the lines follow in the order of the choice; with any other value random permutation is applied to them that preserves the pairs themselves. This makes it possible to present the same pairs in different order and to separate the contribution of the position of rule in the list from the difficulty of particular pair of words. The text is built from distinct words: words to be replaced and background words. The background words are chosen by the generator initialized with the text seed from the vocabulary minus the 2m words of the rules; therefore replacements are absent from the text, and in the right answer every occurrence of replacement corresponds to firing of rule. Each of the words enters the text exactly times, after which the sequence is shuffled by the same generator. Thus all words of the text have the same frequency, and none of them stands out by the statistics of the stream. The stream is broken into lines of ten words without punctuation; the lines serve as anchors in checking the answer (Section 3.4).
