Rules (replace every occurrence of the left word with the right word): {rules} Strict requirements: - Replace only the words listed in the rules. - Do not change, add, or remove any other words. - Keep the exact word order, spaces, and line breaks. 17 - Output only the rewritten text, nothing else. Text: {text} The template is not parameter of the experiment: changing the wording means new version of the protocol, so the wording of the instruction does not act as factor of the outcome. As an example we give published request at the point (D, n, m) = (4, 5, 2)a text of 20 words and two rules: Rules: james -> hang reign -> steal Text: reign cab reign luck cab luck reign reign cab reign james luck james james luck james cab james cab luck Each of the two words to be replaced occurs in the text five times, so the request contains 10 trials. The full prompt and the answer of the model are given in Appendix A. Tasks whose right answer exceeds the answer length limit of the model are not included in the measurement: cutoff of the answer at this limit would be indistinguishable from the degradation of the model. Requests not executed because of technical failure of the provider are also excluded and produce no trials.

sections.title: 3.4 Answer validation
sections.content: Validation turns the answer of the model into sequence of Bernoulli trials: for every occurrence of word to be replaced in the text, the corresponding position of the answer is compared with the reference answer computed by program. Neither an evaluatora person or modelnor measures of text similarity enter the measurement. The reference answer is built in single pass: every occurrence of word to be replaced is replaced by the word assigned to it by rule, and the other words are kept. single pass is enough, because the sets of words to be replaced and of replacements do not overlap, and replacements do not occur in the text. The answer is matched to the reference answer line by line, and the lines serve as synchronization anchors. line with the reference number of words is scored position by position; in line with different number of words the matching initial segment is counted, and the remaining positions are considered unmatchable. The next line is matched anew, so the consequences of local failure are confined to one line. wrong replacement thus remains measured event rather than cause of lost synchronization. Three kinds of deviation of the answer from the reference answer are distinguishedfailures of the first, second and third kind: failure of the first kind is wrong replacement with the structure of the answer preserved; failure of the second kind is local disruption of line (a missing or inserted word), after which the structure of the answer recovers; failure of the third kind is loss of the structure of the answer, after which matching with the lines of the reference answer becomes impossible. 18 The kind of failure characterizes the degree of damage to the answer and is unrelated to errors of the first and second kind in statistical hypothesis testing. Line-by-line matching meets two requirements. First, local failure must not affect the scoring of the rest of the answer: if the answer were compared with the reference answer as single stream, the omission of one word would shift all subsequent positions. Second, the framing of the answer must not shift the matching. Models often supplement the rewritten text with an introductory or closing phrase; without excluding it, flawless answer would be scored as completely wrong. Therefore the lines added before and after the text are excluded, provided that after this the number of lines of the answer matches the reference. The outcome of trial is 1 if the expected replacement stands at the corresponding position of the answer, and 0 in all other cases, including when the position cannot be matched with the reference answer because of failure of the second or third kind. damaged answer is not considered malfunction of the instrument: it gives full measurement, and unmatchable positions are counted as unsuccessful, so the score of the model cannot be overestimated.

sections.title: 3.5 What the instrument measures
sections.content: The result of measurement for every request is the sequence of the outcomes of its trials, taking the values 1 or 0. Every trial is characterized by the number of its rule in the list and the position of the word in the answer, and request by the parameters of the point (D, n, m). These data are primary observations and do not depend on the statistical model used for their analysis. The instrument is defined by the protocolthe vocabulary, the procedure of task construction and the procedure of answer checkingand does not depend on the statistical model. Statistical models are built over the data obtained and can be refined without changing the instrument, and the accumulated data allow repeated analysis. The statistical model used in this work is described in Section 4. This design makes it possible to study the response of model to overload in an arbitrary load range and the influence of each of the load parameters. The points are chosen by the experimenter within the limits set by the size of the vocabulary and the answer length limit of the modelfrom single rule on short text to loads at which the model stops executing the rules entirely. The plan of the experiment is not predetermined by the instrument: varying one parameter with the others fixed, building grid of points and choosing points sequentially from the results of previous measurements are all admissible. Repeated requests are possible at one point. Requests with new seeds realize the same load on different material, which makes it possible to estimate the spread between requests and to smooth out the influence of particular words. Requests with the same pairs of words in different order, set by the order seed, make it possible to separate the contribution of the position of rule in the list from the difficulty of pair of words. Since the task of request is fully determined by six numbers, it can be presented to different models; comparison of models is then carried out on identical tasks, not only at equal load parameters. For the same reason the tasks of published requests are reproducible: any researcher can repeat the measurement on another model or check the published results.

sections.title: 4 The Statistical Model
sections.content: The outcome of an individual trial is random: at one and the same load replacement is executed in some trials and not in others. Therefore the measured quantity is the probability of right 19 replacement as function of the load. It cannot be observed directly: trial gives only 0 or 1, and the probability is estimated only from many trials. The load is multidimensional and is described by several axes. load axis is quantity that is computed from the conditions of trialthe point of the request, the rule number and the position of the word in the answerand describes one side of the load. The relation between the probability and the load is set by statistical modela function of the load axes with finite number of parameters, which are estimated from the outcomes of all trials at once. From the estimated statistical model the characteristics of language model are computed, for example the load at which the share of right replacements falls to given quality level. For such characteristics to make sense, the statistical model must satisfy three requirements: Comparability: characteristic is intended for comparing language models with each other. Since the probability of right replacement depends on the load, characteristics obtained under different conditions would differ not only because of the properties of the language models but also because of the difference in conditions; therefore for all language models characteristic is computed under the same fixed conditions. Moreover, characteristic describes the language model, not the plan of the experiment: measurement of the same model on different set of points must give the same value within the uncertainty. Interpretability: the dependences described by the statistical model must admit an explanation by the properties of the language model. In particular, an increase of the load must not raise the probability of right replacement: such rise, especially in the region of large loads, contradicts the nature of the phenomenon. If the statistical model shows it, this is reason to look for an error in the statistical model itselfin the choice of the axes, in the form of the dependence or in the confounding of the contributions of different axesbefore attributing it to the language model. Applicability beyond the instrument: the axes of the statistical model make sense also for tasks that language models solve outside the instrument. The prompt of an applied task contains set of instructions of different complexity and the input data to which these instructions are applied; the answer of the model is formed on the basis of the input data. The task of the instrument reproduces the same structure in an extremely simplified form: the role of an instruction is played by replacement rule serving as conventional unit of load, the role of the input data by text of vocabulary words, the role of the answer by the transformed text. Consequently, only quantities defined for any prompt of this structure can serve as axes of the statistical model, for example the number of instructions, the position of an instruction in the list, the length of the input text or the position in the answer. Parameters defined only within the instrument, for example the number of repetitions of each word, do not serve as axes.

sections.title: The statistical model must also take into account the properties of the data that follow from
sections.content: the design of the instrument: the outcome of trial is binary; the load axes are linked by the construction of the task: the position of word does not exceed the length of the text, and the rule number does not exceed the number of rules; the trials of one request are linked by the common difficulty of the task; 20 the requests are distributed unevenly over the load space. The form of the dependence of the probability of right replacement on each axis is not known in advance. Therefore the statistical model first measures it from the data, without imposing form, and then describes the measured dependence by smooth laws, from which the characteristics of the language model are computed.

sections.title: 4.1 The Bernoulli trial and the logit
sections.content: The outcome of trial is binary, and every trial is treated as Bernoulli trial: = 1 with probability π and = 0 with probability 1 π, where π is the probability of right replacement in the given trial. The statistical model describes how this probability depends on the load. The probability itself cannot be described by sum of contributions: the probability is bounded by the interval from 0 to 1, and sum of contributions can go beyond it. Therefore the logit is modeledthe logarithm of the odds of right replacement, that is, of the ratio of the probability of right replacement to the probability of wrong one: η = ln π 1 π , π = 1 1 + eη . The logit takes any real value, and the contributions of the load add up in it [16, 4.4]. This meets the requirement of interpretability: every contribution is read separately in common unitthe logitand change of the logit by multiplies the odds of right replacement by e.

sections.title: The logit of trial i of request j is represented as the sum of the contributions of the quantities
sections.content: describing the load and the shift of the request: ηij = θkxijk + bj, bj (0, σ2), where xijk is the value of the k-th quantity describing the load of the trial and θk is its coefficient. The shift bj is one number for all trials of request, reflecting the difficulty of the particular task, that is, of its material. It is introduced because the trials of one request are linked by the common difficulty of the task: without the shift, the spread of task difficulty would not be separated from the contributions of the load. The shift is considered random variable with normal distribution, and its variance σ2 characterizes the spread of request difficulty. logistic model with random shift common to the observations of one group belongs to the generalized linear mixed models (GLMM) [37]. The coefficients θk describe the request that is median in difficulty, with bj = 0, that is, the action of the load on an individual task, as interpretability requires. The share of right replacements taken over all requests is obtained from the same model by averaging over the distribution of the shift; the characteristics comparable between language models are defined through it. The coefficients describing an individual request and the coefficients describing the share over all requests have different scales and are not comparable with each other [2, Sec. VII.C]. The shifts of individual requests are not estimated. The likelihood of every requestthe probability of all its outcomesis averaged over the normal distribution of the shift, and the coefficients θk together with the variance σ2 are found by maximizing this marginal likelihood [37].

sections.title: 4.2 Variables and bins
sections.content: The behavior of language model under load is not known in advance. Therefore the statistical model cannot rely on dependence specified before the measurementlinear or following another 21 law chosen in advance: such model would fit the parameters of given form instead of measuring the form itself. Instead, the values of each axis are divided into intervalsbinsand each bin is assigned its own coefficient, which enters the logit only if the value of the axis falls into this bin. The contribution of the axis to the logit is then piecewise constant, and the form of the dependence is determined by the data [16, 5.15.2]. The dependence of the probability on the load axes is poorly conveyed by bins of equal width, for three reasons: the values of the axes span several orders of magnitude, and bins of equal width would merge the small values into one or two bins and split the rest of the range into many bins; there are fewer data on large values than on small ones: the beginning of the answer and the first rule are present in every request, while distant positions and late rules only in requests with long text and long rule list; the load acts relatively: what matters is by how many times it has grown, not by how much, and in works on load the decline in quality is sometimes close to linear in the logarithm of the load [40]. Therefore logarithmic bins are usedbins of equal width on the logarithmic scale of the axis: the upper boundary of each next bin is twice that of the previous one. Each bin corresponds to one doubling of the value of the axis, the relative precision is the same over the whole range, and the width of the bins grows where there are fewer data, so every bin contains sufficient number of trials. The logit of trial of request in the binned model is written through bin indicators: ηij = X θuk Iuk(xu,ij) + bj, Iuk(x) = (1, Buk, 0, / Buk, where is the number of the axis, the number of bin of this axis, Buk the k-th bin of axis u, xu,ij the value of axis in the trial, θuk the coefficient of the bin, and bj the shift of the request. The bin indicators play the role of the quantities xijk of the formula of Section 4.1: of the sum over the bins of each axis, the coefficient of the bin into which the value of the axis fell remains. The binned representation describes the dependence of the probability on each axis separately by the profile of the coefficients of its bins. Such profile is unique only if the axes are orthogonal: with orthogonal regressors the estimates of the coefficients of one regressor do not depend on the others, while with strongly correlated ones they become unstable [16, 3.2.3]. The load axes are in general not orthogonal, since they are linked by the construction of the task. Therefore requirement analogous to orthogonality is imposed on their set: the statistical model is built on axes whose bin estimates are minimally correlated with each other. The measure is the correlation of the bin estimates of two axes, computed from the covariance of the fit; the values for all pairs of axes are collected in table of axis correlations, and correlation close to one means that the contributions of the two axes are not separated by the data.

sections.title: 4.3 Reference bins and the level
sections.content: In the conventional notation of binned model the logit contains free term α common to all trials: ηij = α + θuk Iuk(xu,ij) + bj. 22 The bins of each axis form partition of its values, so the substitution Iuk(x) = 1 for any x, and for any constant α α + c, θuk θuk for all u = 0; the bin k0 does not change the logit of any trial. The parameters of such notation are not uniquely determined. The redundancy is usually removed by setting the coefficient of one bin of each axis to zero: θuk0 is called the reference bin. Then α is the logit of the median request in the combination of the reference bins of all axes, that is, the level of the model, and the coefficients of the other bins are counted from the reference ones. Only the differences of the coefficients of the bins of one axis are then determined by the data, and the table of estimates gives only comparisons with the reference bin [9]. The choice of the reference bin is arbitrary, and the level depends on it. If instead of bin k0 of axis the bin k1 is made the reference one, the estimates are transformed as follows: α = α + θuk1, θ uk = θuk θuk1, while the logit of every trial remains the same. The data do not distinguish these notations, but the level in them is different. Consequently, α and any quantity counted from it are determined not only by the language model but also by the choice of the coding, which contradicts the requirement of comparability. The second weakness concerns bins in which all outcomes are of one sign. Let all replacements in the bin Buk be right. The derivative of the log-likelihood with respect to the coefficient of this bin, for any value of the shift of the request, ℓ θuk = (cid:0)zij πij (cid:1) = (cid:0)1 πij (cid:1) > 0 xu,ij Buk xu,ij Buk is positive at any finite value of the coefficient; therefore the likelihood, including the marginal one, grows as θuk , and no finite maximum-likelihood estimate exists. For bin where all replacements are wrong, the same holds as θuk . This is special case of the general condition for the existence of maximum-likelihood estimates in logistic regression [1]. Such bin is excluded from the fit together with its trials, and the check is repeated until there is nothing left to exclude. It is natural to choose the bin of the smallest loads as the reference one, but it is precisely in the combination of the smallest loads that there may be no errors at all; then the reference bin is excluded, and the level α is not determined by the data. Therefore our statistical model has no free term: the logit has the form given in Section 4.2. The level in it is not tied to any individual bin, and bins in which all outcomes are of one sign are excluded without harm to the determinacy of the model. Between the axes the same redundancy remains as between α and the bins: the common constant of the logit can be moved from the bins of one axis to the bins of another without changing the logit of any trial, and it is removed by an arbitrary condition. Consequently, the data determine only the shape of the profile of each axis, that is, the differences between the coefficients of its bins, but not its shift. The shifts of all profiles are established later from the smooth laws drawn through the bins, and only then is the level determined.

sections.title: 4.4 Approximation shift correction
sections.content: The profile of the coefficients of the bins serves as an estimate of the dependence of the probability on the axis that is free of assumptions about its form. smooth law is fitted to this estimate as model with fewer parameters: the parameters of the law are chosen so that the values of the law in 23 the bins are closest to the bin estimates in the metric given by the covariance of these estimates. Such two-step schemefirst free, reduced-form parameters, then structural parameters linked to them by known mappingis classical minimum distance estimation [30, 1, 2.2.4]. It makes it possible to choose the form of the law from the measured profile rather than to specify it in advance. The parameters of the law of axis are found by minimizing the distance ˆψu = arg min ψu (cid:2)ˆθu hu(ψu)(cid:3)T ˆΩ1 (cid:2)ˆθu hu(ψu)(cid:3), where ˆθu is the vector of estimates of the coefficients of the bins of the axis, ˆΩu is their covariance obtained in the fit, and hu(ψu) is the vector of values of the law with parameters ψu in the same bins. The weight matrix inverse to the covariance of the reduced-form parameters is optimal: with it the estimates of the structural parameters have the smallest asymptotic variance among minimum distance estimates [30, 5.2]. Bins excluded from the fit (Section 4.3) have no estimate and do not enter the distance. The parameters of the law are uniquely determined by the remaining bins if different parameter values give different values of the law in the bins; for this the number of bins with an estimate must be no smaller than the number of parameters of the law [30, 2.2.4]. The fit of the bins determines the shape of the profile of each axis, but not the level at which the profile lies. As shown in Section 4.3, the coefficients of the bins of one axis can be increased and those of another decreased by the same amount without changing the logit of any trial. Therefore the level at which the bins of each axis end up is set by an arbitrary condition of the fit, not by the data. An additional restriction that fixes such constant and makes the parameters uniquely determined is called normalization [30, 2.2, footnote 11]. The law of an axis is fitted with free constant terma normalization constant. While the other parameters describe the shape of the profile, the normalization constant takes the level at which the bins ended up. Then the arbitrary normalization is replaced by meaningful one: the law, together with the bins of the axis, is shifted so that the law vanishes at the smallest load along this axis. The size of this shift is called the shift of the profile. If at vanishing load the law converges asymptotically to horizontal line, the shift equals the level of this asymptote. If the law is defined at the minimum load, the shift equals its value at this load. After the shift, the profile of each axis shows the change of the logit relative to the smallest load along this axis. The shift δu of axis is subtracted from the coefficients of all its bins, and the sum of the shifts of all axes forms the reference level of the statistical model: θuk = θuk δu, αphys = δu, ηij = αphys + θuk Iuk(xu,ij) + bj. trial falls into exactly one bin of each axis, so the shift of each axis is subtracted from its logit, and the level returns their sum: the logit of no trial changes. The normalization constant of the law is free, so the shift of an axis moves together with its bins: however the common constant of the logit was distributed between the axes in the fit, the corrected bins and the level do not depend on it. The parameters of the laws, the shifts and the level are functions of the estimates of the coefficients of the bins, and their uncertainties are determined by the covariance of the fit. The covariance of these quantities is obtained by the delta methodlinearization of the function at the point of the estimate: Cov(cid:0)g(ˆθ)(cid:1) Σ gT, where ˆθ are the estimates of the coefficients, Σ their covariance, and the matrix of derivatives of at the point ˆθ. For the parameters of law with the optimal weight matrix the linearization (cid:1)1, where Gu is the matrix of derivatives of the values gives the asymptotic covariance (cid:0)GT of the law in the bins with respect to its parameters [30, Theorem 3.2]. Gu ˆΩ1 The approximation correction removes the indeterminacy left by the fit of the bins. level appears again in the statistical modelthe reference level αphys, the logit of right replacement for the median request at the smallest load along all axes. Unlike the level α of the conventional notation, which depends on the choice of reference bins (Section 4.3), the reference level does not depend on the coding: it is determined by the data through the laws of the axes. All bins are corrected by the approximation curves: each curve either converges asymptotically to zero at vanishing load along its axis or crosses zero at the point of minimum load (D, n, m) = (4, 5, 1). The contributions of all axes are now counted from one statethe smallest loadand express in logits the price of the load along each axis. Therefore the contributions of different axes are comparable with each other, and their sum shows what part of the reference level given load spends.

sections.title: 4.5 The notion of instruction capacity
sections.content: Definition. The statistical model describes how the probability of right replacement depends on the load. characteristic of language model is the inverse quantitythe load at which this probability falls to given quality level q. The probability of right replacement depends on all load axes at once, so such load is defined only at fixed values of the other axes. For it to be comparable between language models, the other axes are fixed at the smallest load x0in the same state in which the reference level is defined (Section 4.4). The instruction execution capacity, or instruction capacity (Instruction Execution Capacity, IEC), IECq is the number of rules at which the probability of right replacement in this state equals q, that is, the solution of the equation π(m; x0) = with respect to m. This is the inverse problem of regression: from the estimated dependence of response on In this way, an exposure, the exposure at which the response reaches given value is found. in doseresponse analysis the effective dose is determinedthe dose at which the probability of response equals given valueand the ratio of the effective doses of two curves serves as measure for comparing two substances [38, Sec. Inverse regression]. The capacity is expressed in conventional units of loadrules. Unlike the effective input length, which is chosen from the tested lengths (Section 2.2), it is continuous quantity with an uncertainty. We use two quality levels: = 0.95 corresponds to reliable execution of the rules, = 0.5 to the level at which only half of the replacements are right. The quality level refers to the share of right replacements over all requests, whereas the coefficients of the statistical model describe the request that is median in difficulty (Section 4.1). The share over all requests at the logit η of the median request is obtained by averaging over the distribution of the shift of request: π(η) = φ(b; 0, σ2) 1 + e(η+b) db, where φ(b; 0, σ2) is the density of the normal distribution of the shift. The transition from the probabilities of an individual group of trials to the probabilities over the whole population of groups by integrating over the random effect is known technique for random-effects models [19, 25 Sec. 3]. Therefore on the logit scale the level corresponds to thresholdthe logit of the median request η(q, σ2) at which the share over all requests equals q: π(cid:0)η(q, σ2)(cid:1) = q, and the condition the share of right replacements is not below is equivalent to the condition η η(q, σ2). At σ2 = 0 the threshold coincides with the logit of the quality level Lq = ln 1 : L0.95 = ln 19 2.94 and L0.5 = 0. At = 0.5 the threshold is zero for any variance of the shift: the logistic function is symmetric, 1/(1 + ex) = 1 1/(1 + ex), and with symmetric distribution of the shift the share over all requests at zero logit of the median request equals exactly 0.5. At = 0.95 the threshold grows with the variance of the shift. Consequently, IEC0.5 does not depend on the spread of request difficulty, while IEC0.95 does. The same definition applies to any axis along which the load accumulates, for example to the position of word in the answer or to the length of the text. The capacity along such an axis is its value at which the share of right replacements falls to q, and this capacity is expressed in the units of its axis. Capacities along different axes have different units and do not add up. The capacity in the number of rules shows how many rules language model holds at once, and the capacity in the position in the answer how long it applies them over the course of the answer. Computation. The difference between the reference level and the threshold = αphys η(q, σ2) is called the reserve of the level: by this many logits the load can lower the logit of the reference state before the share of right replacements falls to q. At = 0.5 the whole reference level serves as the reserve. In logistic model with linear predictor η = β0 + β1x and without the shift of request, the solution of the inverse problem is written explicitly, xq = (β0 Lq)/(β1): the exposure spends the reserve β0 Lq at β1 per unit. The capacity is built in the same way, but the load is rules, and each next rule has its own price. The price a(r) of the rule with number is the decrease of the logit brought by adding this rule to the table; what it consists of is determined by the axes of the statistical model. The first rule is present in any task, so it enters the reference level and has no price. Rules with different numbers cost differently, and their prices add up one by one: the cumulative price of table of rules equals C(m) = a(r). The capacity is the largest number of rules whose cumulative price fits into the reserve, with the fraction of the rule at which the reserve is exhausted: r=2 IECq = m0 + C(m0) a(m0 + 1) , m0 = max{ : C(m) }. The fraction of the last rule makes the capacity continuous quantity. If the cumulative price is given by smooth law, the capacity is the root of the equation C(m) = q; such equations are in general solved numerically [38, Sec. Inverse regression]. The capacity along another axis is 26 computed in the same wayas the root of the equation Cu(x) = q, where Cu is the cumulative price of the load along this axis. Within the region of loads represented in the measurement, the capacity is measured. If the reserve is not exhausted by the edge of this region, the capacity by the smooth law is obtained by extrapolation and is marked as an extrapolation. By the bins there is no price of rule beyond the last bin, and only lower bound of the capacity is knownthe edge of the measured region. The capacity is computed in two ways: by the corrected bins, where the prices are given by the coefficients of the bins, and by the smooth laws. The first computation shows what is measured, the second what the accepted form of the dependence gives, and the discrepancy between them serves as measure of the quality of the approximation. Uncertainty. The capacity is function of the estimates of the statistical model, and its uncertainty, like the uncertainty of an effective dose [38, Sec. Inverse regression], is obtained by the delta method (Section 4.4). The capacity is given by the equation C(m) = implicitly, so its derivative with respect to the estimates θ, which here include the variance of the shift σ2, is found by differentiating this equation: IECq θ = C/θ q/θ C/m . The variance of the shift enters the capacity uncertainty only through the threshold: q/σ2 = η/σ2. At = 0.5 this derivative is zero, and the uncertainty of the estimate of σ2 does not enter IEC0.5.

sections.title: 5 The Passport of GPT-4o mini
sections.content: The experimental instrument and the statistical model described in the previous sections were used for systematic study of the behavior of the GPT-4o mini language model under controlled load. The results obtained make it possible to identify the factors that determine the gradual degradation of the quality of instruction following and the occurrence of failures of the third kind, and to establish quantitative regularities of the influence of each of these factors.

sections.title: 5.1 The measurement
sections.content: The language model GPT-4o mini, presented by OpenAI on 18 July 2024 as the most cost-efficient of its small models [32], was chosen as the object of measurement. The study was carried out on the version gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18 with context window of 128 000 tokens and maximum answer length of 16 384 tokens [33]. These limits were taken into account when forming the tasks: in particular, the full right answer had to fit within the answer length limit of the model (Section 3.3). The same generation parameters were used for all requests, chosen so as to minimize the variability of the answers unrelated to the content of the task. The temperature was set to zero, and the seed parameter was fixed at the value 20260907, which made it possible to increase the reproducibility of the results when the same task was presented again. The value top_p = 1 excluded an additional restriction of the choice of tokens by cumulative probability. The max_tokens parameter was set to 16 384, that is, to the maximum value admissible for this model, so that the settings of the request would not introduce additional restrictions on the length of the generated answer. The scale of the measurements characterizes the computational costs needed to study one model. The measurement covered 1890 experimental points and included 2958 requests, each of which received an answer. The points of the measurement were chosen by closed adaptive planning 27 technology (Section 8). The length of the presented texts ranged from 20 to 10 240 words, and the number of rules in task from 1 to 256. The total number of trials (words requiring replacement) was 642 430. According to the counters of the provider, during the measurements the model processed 7 850 106 input tokens and generated 8 091 766 output tokens. The total running time of the instrument was 5 43 min.

sections.title: 5.2 Choice of the axes of the predictor model
sections.content: The axes of the predictor model were chosen sequentially, by testing alternative sets of axes. The goal was to find coordinate system that would make it possible to estimate the main factors of degradation separately and to predict the probability of correct execution of an individual trial, including at experimental points that did not take part in the fit of the statistical model. Initially parametric statistical model was used in which the probability of right replacement depended on five axes: the length of the text = Dn, where is the number of distinct words and is the number of repetitions of each word; the number of distinct words D; the number of rules m; the ordinal number of the checked rule and the position of the word of the trial in the generated answer s, counted from one. In addition, two interactions were taken into account: of the number of rules with the length of the text and with the number of distinct words. The dependences on and were set by analytic functions chosen in advance. The first results cast doubt on the validity of this choice of functional forms. In particular, the experimental data did not allow reliably distinguishing linear and logarithmic dependence on the length of the text. Using single slope in also led to carrying the regularities measured at small values of this axis over to the region of large values without sufficient experimental confirmation. Therefore the next step was the transition from functions set in advance to free binned parametrization, which makes it possible to estimate the profile of the influence of each axis directly from the data. However, even after this the contribution of the number of distinct words remained hard to interpret: an increase of was accompanied by an increase of the probability of right replacement, as if greater lexical diversity made the task easier. An analysis of the construction of the task showed that at fixed length of the text an increase of simultaneously decreases the number of repetitions of each word = v/D. Thus the original axis in fact also reflected the inverse dependence on repetitiveness. For more natural interpretation of the load it was replaced by the number of repetitions n. This replacement did not add new information, since for known the parameters and are uniquely expressed through each other, but it made it possible to represent the observed effect differently. At the same time one more problem of the original coordinate system came to light. Significant interaction terms showed that the influence of the number of rules depends on the length of the text. This agreed with the assumption that the rule table and the processed text compete for limited resources of the model and indicated that the load in the chosen coordinates cannot be satisfactorily represented by sum of independent contributions. To achieve more stable separation of the factors, we moved from describing task through its constructive parameters to describing individual trials with regard to the order of their execution. The new statistical model used three axes: the number of rules m, the number of the checked rule and the event number gthe ordinal number of the current trial among all trials of the request, including itself. These axes described, respectively, the size of the rule table, the position of rule in the table and the progress of the model through the sequence of replacements. The contributions of the three axes were well separated, but the statistical model contained no explicit characteristic of the total volume of the processed text. As result, the degradation 28 related to its increase was partly attributed to the number of rules, since in the experimental data these quantities changed together. Therefore the length of the text was returned to the statistical model. The opposite approach was also considereddescribing request exclusively by its original parameters D, and m. However, such statistical model did not take into account the position of an individual trial in the sequence of execution of the task and, consequently, did not make it possible to separate the overall load of the request from its change as the answer is generated. The next essential step was the introduction of the replacement density , = defined as the share of distinct words of the text for which replacement rules are given. The need for this axis became apparent when comparing tasks with the same number of rules but different lexical composition. For example, with eight rules and eight distinct words the model correctly executed approximately half of the replacements, whereas with the same eight rules and 64 distinct words practically all of them, even though the first text was shorter than the second. Consequently, the absolute number of rules does not characterize the load they create without taking into account what share of the words requires the application of rules. The introduction of the density made it possible to form new triple of task coordinates: the length of the text v, the replacement density and the number of rules m. To check the validity of this choice, we compared it with alternative parametrizations. Returning to the original parameters D, and improved the separability of the estimates but worsened the quality of the description of the experimental data and the accuracy of prediction at points that did not take part in the fit. Including and together with v, and also gave no new information, since the original parameters are uniquely recovered from the new ones: = , = m . Additional interaction terms improved the description of the data used in the fit but did not provide corresponding improvement of the forecast at new points. Based on the totality of these results, the triple v, p, was chosen to characterize the load of request as whole. After the task coordinates were chosen, it remained to determine which axes are needed to describe an individual trial. Besides the rule number and the event number already used, the position of word in the answer and the application number of rule kthe ordinal number of the current application of the given rule among all its applications in the requestwere tested. It turned out that these quantities contain considerable share of common information. The position of word approximately corresponded to the ratio g/p, and the application number of rule to the ratio g/m. When the axes were included together, even singling out the residual contributions of and not explained by these dependences did not improve the forecast at new experimental points. This created the need to choose the most suitable coordinate of progress through the answer, rather than keep several axes that mainly describe the same process. Separately, the possibility of using the position of word instead of the total length of the text was tested. Such representation worsened the quality of the description of the data and led to strong mutual dependence of the position, the event number and the replacement density. This confirmed the need to distinguish between the total volume of the presented text and the position of an individual trial in the generated answer. An additional difficulty in separating the factors was the interrelation of the length of the text and the replacement density, caused by the very construction of the tasks: very small values of the density are attainable only with sufficiently long text. To separate more explicitly the progress 29 through the sequence of trials from the influence of the intermediate words that do not require replacement, an auxiliary axis was introducedthe excess background: = + 1 + 1 , = mn, where is the total number of trials in the request. The quantity characterizes the deviation of the actual position of the checked word from the expected position of the corresponding trial under random placement of the trials in the text. It was assumed that such coordinate would make it possible to single out better the influence of the background text without mixing it with the ordinal number of the replacement being executed. To test this hypothesis, series of experiments was carried out in which Q, g, and were simultaneously included in the statistical model, after which individual axes were excluded one by one. It turned out that the profile of the excess background does not retain an independent stable form and in fact is mixture of the contributions of the length of the text and the position of the word. The event number and the position also described mainly the same progress through the answer. When was excluded, the dependence on acquired more regular profile, whereas the contribution of the rule number remained stable in all the parametrization variants tested. These results determined the choice of two coordinates of an individual trial: the rule number and the position of the word s. The event number g, the application number of rule and the excess background did not provide an independent stable contribution that would justify keeping them alongside the chosen axes. To check the completeness of the resulting system, one more possible axis was considered the position of the checked word in the full context c, defined by the number of tokens from the beginning of the prompt to the corresponding word in the answer, including the instruction and the rule table. This axis contained additional information but could replace neither the length of the text nor the position of the word s. Therefore it was not included in the main set of five axes and remained candidate for further extension of the statistical model. Finally, the need to keep the number of rules as an independent coordinate was checked again. When it was excluded, the corresponding contribution was redistributed between the replacement density and the rule number, which confirmed the need to take into account explicitly. Reincluding the number of repetitions and the application number of rule revealed no new factors improving the statistical model. Thus, as result of the sequential comparison of alternative parametrizations, set of five axes of the predictor model was chosen: the length of the word list = Dn; Sthe ordinal number of word in the list s, counted from one; the replacement density = m/D; the number of rules m; Rthe ordinal number of the checked rule in the table r. For the GPT-4o mini language model, the chosen coordinate system is the most complete of the sets of axes studied with low mutual correlation  (Table 3)  . The chosen coordinate system makes it possible to characterize both the overall load of task and the heterogeneity of its action on individual trials. The comparative experiments carried out 30 Table 3: Correlations of the axes of the predictor model from the data of the GPT-4o mini measurement: the canonical correlation of the increments of the coefficients of neighboring bins of two axes. P 1 0.33 0.76 0.53 0.15 0.33 1 0.41 0.22 0.36 0.76 0.41 1 0.45 0. 0.53 0.22 0.45 1 0.42 0.15 0.36 0.10 0.42 1 confirm the sufficiency of the five-axis parametrization: the additional axes tested did not provide an independent contribution justifying further complication of the statistical model. In the statistical model with separate axes, the contributions of the length of the word list and of the position of the word are represented additively. Consequently, doubling of the length should lead to the same change of the logit regardless of the position of the word in the answer. However, the measurements showed that the size of this change depends substantially on the position: at the beginning of the answer the decrease of the logit when the length doubles is 1.41.8, whereas deep in the answer it approaches zero. Such behavior cannot be described by sum of two independent contributions. Therefore the separate axes and were combined into two-dimensional grid in which each combination of length and position bins has its own free coefficient. Thus, in the statistical model of the passport the joint influence of length and position is represented by single term: ηij = S(v, s) + (p) + (m) + R(r) + bj, where S(v, s) is the coefficient of the cell of the two-dimensional grid corresponding to the given trial, and (p), (m) and R(r) are the coefficients of the bins of the other axes. After the notation of its axes, the model was named VS-PMR. In this parametrization length and position enter the model jointly, not as two independent terms.

sections.title: 5.3 Laws and observations
sections.content: From the results of the GPT-4o mini measurement, the fit of the VS-PMR statistical model gave the profiles of the coefficients of the bins of all load axes. The form of these profiles was not set in advance, yet each of them turned out to be regular and is described by smooth law with small number of parameters, whose form is determined by the shape of the profile itself. These laws are the regularities found: each of them expresses how the load factor described by the axis lowers the probability of right replacement.

The grid law obtained admits clear geometric interpretation. In the coordinates of the contribution to the logit and the logarithm of the word position, all slices have the form of hyperbola with common slanted asymptote. They differ only by the height of the horizontal plateau: the load by the text volume cuts off the upper part of one and the same descending dependence at the level µv, and the hyperbola provides smooth transition from the plateau to the slanted part. Thus an increase of the volume does not shift the whole profile down but changes the level of its upper bound. The height of this bound is determined by the length of the text. Before the transition region near the plateau level hardly depends on the length, and beyond it the level decreases by an approximately constant amount with every doubling of v, that is, linearly in the logarithm of the volume. Since the slanted asymptote remains unchanged, lowering the plateau simultaneously shifts the intersection point of the asymptotes to later word positions: for the slice of 4180 words the asymptotes intersect around the 80th word of the answer, and for the slice of 512110 240 words around the 600th. Therefore, as the text volume grows, the plateau becomes at the same time 36 lower and longer. progress through the answer but is direct geometric consequence of lowering the cutoff level. Its greater length does not testify to greater robustness of the model to Beyond the transition region the profiles of all slices converge to the common slanted asymptote, and the contribution of the grid is determined practically exclusively by the word position s, regardless of the text length v. Consequently, the law found describes not an accumulation of two independent losses but an interaction of two limits. The text volume sets the upper level of the quality of instruction following, which shows itself already at the beginning of the answer, whereas the word position sets the general regularity of its subsequent decrease. As long as the positional limit is weaker than the volume one, the profile stays on the plateau. When it becomes stricter, the further decrease is determined by the word position, and the initial differences between texts of different length gradually disappear. This is precisely what explains the observed convergence of the profiles deep in the answer. The dependences found admit mechanistic interpretation. The limit associated with the axis may reflect decrease in the reliability of processing the task as whole as the volume of the input data grows. Presumably, up to certain region of load the model is able to process the presented volume without noticeable additional loss of quality, after which every doubling of it is accompanied by an approximately equal decrease of the logit. Such an effect may be associated both with limits on holding the input information and with interference between the elements of large input text. The common dependence on the position is of different nature: it shows itself as the answer progresses and hardly depends on the full volume of the text. One possible explanation is the growing distance between the current place of generation and the rule list located at the beginning of the prompt. As the answer is formed this distance grows, which may make it harder to refer to the needed rule and apply it correctly. This hypothesis agrees with the earlier established independent informational contribution of the absolute position of the word in the full context beyond the text length and the position in the answer (Section 5.2). Thus the results point to the existence of two qualitatively different limits of instruction execution: volume limit, which determines the available initial level, and positional limit, which determines the subsequent decrease. Their interaction is described with good accuracy by smoothed minimum, not by sum of independent penalties. At the same time, the form and the quantitative characteristics of the dependences have been established experimentally, but not the mechanisms underlying them. The interpretations proposed require separate experimental test.

sections.content: The coefficients of the replacement density bins = m/D obtained by the fit are shown in Figure 5. Each bin is plotted at the mean density of its trials; the bins span the range from the density 1/512 to the full density = 1, at which every word of the text is replaced, and none of them is excluded from the fit. As with the grid, the level at which the coefficients lie is set by an arbitrary condition of the fit (Section 4.3): the density bin 1/41/2 is pinned at zero by this condition and has no uncertainty of its own, and only the shape of the profile is meaningful. At low density the coefficients are constant within the uncertainties: for the bins up to density of about 1/16 they lie between 3.9 and 4.7. From this density on the profile decreases, and at full density the coefficient falls to 4.8. On the logarithmic density axis the profile has horizontal asymptote at rare replacements and then falls steeply. This shape is described by the law of exponential saturation where (p) = µP AP 37 (cid:0)1 ep/pc(cid:1), Figure 5: Coefficients of the replacement density bins and the density law before the shift correction. The law was fitted to the coefficients of nine bins with weights inverse to their full covariance, as in Section 4.4; the bin pinned by the condition of the fit does not enter the distance. The fit gave AP = 12.07 2.63 and pc = 0.67 0.27, and the curve of the law in Figure 5 passes through the bins within their uncertainties. By the rule of Section 4.4 the shift of the density profile equals the level of this asymptote: δP = µP = 4.45 0.70. The normalization constant of the law is µP , and after subtracting the shift the law takes the form eP (p) = (p) δP = AP (cid:0)1 ep/pc (cid:1), that is, it expresses the loss of the logit relative to rare replacements. The shift δP is subtracted from the coefficients of all density bins and passes into the reference level αphys (Section 4.4); the logit of no trial changes. The corrected bins are shown in Figure 6. After the correction the profile at rare replacements lies at zero, and each bin shows the change of the contribution of the density to the logit relative Figure 6: Replacement density bins and the density law after the shift correction: δP = µP is subtracted from all bins. The notation is the same as in Figure 5. to rare replacements, with the other terms of the statistical model unchanged. At the density 1/16 the loss is about one logit, and at full density, when every word of the text is replaced, it reaches (cid:0)1 e1/pc(cid:1) = 9.35 1.01 logits. This is about 78% of the limiting loss AP : saturation is not AP reached in the measured region, and the loss keeps growing up to full density. The density law admits simple reading. At low density 1 ep/pc p/pc, and the loss is proportional to the share of the words of the text requiring replacement: it grows at the rate AP /pc 18 logits per unit of density, that is, about 0.18 logits per percent of replaced words. Therefore on the logarithmic axis rare replacements cost almost nothing as long as their share does not exceed few percent, after which the loss grows rapidly. On the linear density scale the growth of the loss slows down as full density is approached, and the law tends to the limit AP , which the measured region does not reach. The form of the law admits an interpretation through limited throughput. While replacements are rare, each of them is executed almost without loss, and as the share of the words requiring the application of rules grows, the replacements begin to compete for the limited ability of the language model to apply rules in the course of the answer, and the loss grows. The factor 1 ep/pc has simple probabilistic meaning here. The words of the text are arranged in random order, and the share of positions requiring replacement equals p; therefore the probability of meeting another word to be replaced among the nearest 1/pc words is approximately 1 ep/pc. With the value of pc found, this window is about one and half words, from one to two and half with the uncertainty taken into account: the loss grows together with the probability that the neighboring word also requires replacement. The saturation of the law at the level AP corresponds to the limit of throughput: when almost every word to be replaced has another one as neighbor, further growth of the density adds few new collisions. similar dependence has been studied for flows of many bodies along paths of limited capacity. In single-file pedestrian movement the speed of each pedestrian is determined by the length requiredthe distance to the one walking ahead, which on average is inverse to the density of the flowand the speed decreases as the density grows; this dependence of speed on density, called the fundamental diagram, serves as quantitative measure of the capacity of walking paths [39]. In the task of the instrument the role of this distance is played by the gap between neighboring words to be replaced, on average equal to 1/p words, and the quantity 1/pc sets the scale of the gap at which the loss reaches 63% of its limit. Separating the contribution of the density from the contribution of the text length requires care. Density and length form the most strongly linked pair of axes of the statistical model  (Table 3)  : very small density is attainable only in long text, so the horizontal asymptote at rare replacements is determined mainly by long texts, and its separation from the contribution of the length relies on the additivity of the contributions of the density and the grid in the statistical model. The instrument measures the form of the dependence, but not its cause, and the interpretation proposed requires separate test. Thus the replacement density acts as an independent load factor: the loss of the logit grows with the share of the words requiring replacement, becomes noticeable from density of the order of few percent and at full density reaches about nine logits relative to rare replacements.

In works where the quality of instruction following is measured as function of the number of instructions [21, 15], these contributions are not separated: as the number of instructions grows, both the size of the list and the numbers of the instructions checked in it grow at the same time. dependence linear in the logarithm of the number of elements held simultaneously is known for holding keyvalue correspondences: the recall accuracy decreases approximately linearly in the logarithm of the number of tracked keys and of the number of their updates, which the authors associate with general limit on the resistance of language model to mutual interference [40]. sections.title: 5.4 Collapse of the answer
sections.content: A collapse of the answer is request whose answer ended with failure of the third kind (Section 3.4), that is, with loss of the structure of the answer. failure of the third kind takes two forms. In the first, the model skips, merges or adds lines in the middle of the answer, and the lines following them end up not at their numbers. In the second, the answer is cut off: it is incomplete, and the last lines of the text are missing from it. In both cases we will say that the request lost the text. All replacements after the place of the failure, including those in the missing lines, are counted as unsuccessful. In the GPT-4o mini measurement 995 requests out of 2958 lost the text, that is, 33.6%. wrong replacement is an event of an individual trial, whereas collapse is an event of the request as whole: after the place where the text is lost, the outcome of every trial is zero, whatever rule is checked in it. Therefore collapse has two measurable characteristics of its own: the probability that request loses the text, and the place in the answer at which this happens. 45 Each of them is described by its own law: the collapse rate in Section 5.4.1, the place of the collapse in Section 5.4.2. 5.4.1 Collapse rate Let ψ denote the probability that request loses the text. Each request is treated as one Bernoulli trial with the outcome text lost or text kept, and the law of the collapse rate describes how ψ depends on the load of the request. The fit of the law also included requests that did not enter the fit of the statistical model: such requests describe not the capacity but the collapse of the answer (Section 5.3.3), and it is precisely for the collapse law that they are informative. The form of the law was chosen from the binned representation: logistic model of the outcomes of requests with bins of the text length and the replacement density (Section 4.2). The reference bins are the length bin of 4180 words, the shortest of the bins in which both outcomes occur, and the density bin 1/41/2, as in the statistical model. Bins all of whose requests have one outcome have no estimate and are excluded together with their requests: texts up to 40 words (35 requests, all kept the text) and the density 1/10241/512 (6 requests, all lost it). The coefficients of the length bins grow approximately linearly with the bin number, that is, linearly in the logarithm of the length. The coefficients of the density bins are almost constant at densities up to 1/32 and then grow steeply towards full density. If bins of the number of rules are added to the model, their coefficients lie within 0.5 logits of zero and do not change systematically with the number of rules: only for one bin out of eight, 58 rules, does the 95% interval not include zero, which with eight bins agrees with random scatter. This shape is described by the law ln ψ 1 ψ = λψ + κψ log2 20 + Aψ pγψ , where λψ is the logit of the collapse at the shortest text of the measurement, = 20 words, and vanishing density, 0; κψ is the slope in logits per doubling of the text length; Aψ is the contribution of the density to the logit of the collapse at full density, = 1; γψ is the exponent that sets how fast the contribution of the density grows with p. The law was built in the same way as the laws of the axes of the statistical model. First, the coefficients of the length and density bins were found by maximum likelihood from the outcomes of the requests. The requests are distributed unevenly over the load space (Section 4), so each request entered the likelihood with weight inverse to the number of requests in its cellthe combination of the bins of length, density and number of rules. With such weights all cells contribute equally to the fit, and the law describes the language model, not the plan of the experiment. The uncertainties of the coefficients were computed from the sandwich covariance, which remains consistent also with weighted likelihood [2]. Then the law of each axis was drawn through the coefficients of its bins: the straight line Vψ(v) = λV ψ + κψ log2(v/20) through the length bins and the curve Pψ(p) = µP ψ + Aψ pγψ through the density bins. The density law was fitted with weights inverse to the full covariance of the bins, as in Section 4.4. The length bins are counted from one reference bin and are strongly correlated through it, and with such weights the line drifted away from all the bins; therefore, as for the grid (Section 5.3.1), the weights of the length law were the inverses of the variances of the bins, and the 46 uncertainties were computed from the full covariance by the delta method. By the rule of Section 4.4 the shift of the length equals the value of the law at the smallest length of the measurement, = 20 words: λV ψ = 3.64 2.12. The fit gave λψ = 20.001.58, κψ = 2.400.19, Aψ = 12.251.01 and γψ = 0.71 0.09. The number of rules does not enter the law, although the share of collapses taken over the requests with given number of rules grows with the number of rules. The growth is explained by the construction of the task: at one and the same density task with more rules contains more distinct words, = m/p, and therefore has longer text, = Dn. All nine requests with 256 rules lost the text. Consequently, at given text length and replacement density the number of rules does not affect the probability of the collapse. The length law admits simple probabilistic reading. If the model lost the text on each line of the answer with one and the same small probability, independently of the other lines, the probability of the collapse, while it is small, would be proportional to the number of lines, and each doubling 47 Figure 12: Text length bins and the length law after the shift correction: λV ψ is subtracted from all bins. The notation is the same as in Figure 11. of the text length would increase the logit of the collapse by ln 2 0.69. The measured slope κψ is 3.5 times larger: the odds of the collapse grow approximately in proportion to the text length to the power 3.5, (v/20)κψ/ ln 2 = (v/20)3.5. Consequently, the risk of losing the text on the next line is not constant but growseither as the answer progresses or with the volume of the whole text. Which of these causes acts is shown by the place of the collapse (Section 5.4.2). The independence of the collapse from the number of rules separates it from the limit that the instruction capacity measures. doubling of the rule list lowers the logit of right replacement by κM = 0.43 (Section 5.3.3), but does not change the probability of losing the text at an unchanged length and density. The collapse is determined by the load of the textits length and the share of the words requiring replacementand not by the number of instructions held. The rules determine which word to write in place of the word to be replaced, but not where in the text the model is; apparently, applying rules and keeping the place in the text load different sides of the work of the model. The dependences found admit mechanistic interpretation. The task of the instrument requires rewriting the text line by line, and the model composes most of the answer by copying the input. In transformers, copying previously encountered sequences is performed by induction heads: such head finds the place in the input where the current token and the few preceding ones occurred, and raises the probability of the token that stood next there, by the scheme [A][B] . . . [A] [B] [31]. With such mechanism the place in the text is determined by the coincidence of the end of the answer already written with fragment of the input. This mechanism explains the dependence of the collapse on the density. The replacement words do not occur in the source text, so each such word written in the answer breaks the coincidence of the last words of the answer with the corresponding fragment of the input text. In sparse text such breaks are isolated: the answer repeats the input almost verbatim, and the place in the text is found by the neighboring copied words. As the density grows, the share of the words of the answer absent from the text grows together with p, and at the density = 1 not single word of the answer occurs in the input, and the place in the text has to be held without relying on verbatim match. This may explain the steep growth of the contribution of the density as full density is approached. The dependence on the length agrees with observations of long generation. In LongGenBench the fulfilment of requirements tied to places of the answer worsens as the answer grows longer, and on the transition from 16 to 32 thousand tokens the models more often fail to finish the answer [43]; an unfinished answer corresponds to the second form of failure of the third kind. For GPT-4o mini the loss of the text becomes frequent already at text lengths of the order of thousand words, and the slope κψ serves as quantitative measure of this effect. The instrument measures the form of the dependence, but not its cause, and the interpretations proposed require separate test. Thus the collapse rate is determined by the load of the text: the odds of losing the text grow approximately in proportion to its length to the power 3.5 and rise steeply with the replacement density above 1/16, while the number of rules at given length and density does not affect them. The collapse of the text and the instruction capacity are different limits of language model.

sections.title: 5.4.2 Place of the collapse
sections.content: Let denote the probability that for request that lost the text, the text is already lost by the word with number s. The place where the text is lost is the line from which the answer stops following the text line by line: the first line of the text after the last line of the answer that stands at its own number, if further on in the answer there are lines of the text with shifted numbers, and for cut-off answer the first missing line. Each word to be replaced of request that lost the text is treated as Bernoulli trial with the outcome 1 if its line does not precede the place where the text is lost, and 0 otherwise. The fit included all 995 requests that lost the text and their 365 955 words to be replaced, of which 49.2% stand at or after the place where the text is lost. The probability is described in the same way as the collapse rate. The logit of is decomposed by the bins of three axes: the word number (the position bins of the grid, Section 5.3.1), the replacement density and the share of the text passed before the word, (s 1)/v, divided into ten equal bins. The reference bins are the bin of words 6411280, which has the most trials, the density bin 1/41/2 and the first bin of the text share; there are no bins with one outcome. Each request entered the likelihood with weight inverse to the number of requests that lost the text in its cell, and the uncertainties of the coefficients were computed from the cluster sandwich covariance with the cluster one request [2]. The law of each axis was drawn through the coefficients of its bins. The profile of the word number has horizontal plateau at the beginning of the answer and slanted rise after the corner, that is, the same form as the plateau level of the grid as function of the text length (Section 5.3.1), but with rise instead of decline. It is described by the hyperbola SF (s) = µSF + κSF 2 log s + log2 2 + ω SF , where µSF is the level of the horizontal asymptote to which the profile tends at the beginning of the answer; κSF is the slope of the slanted asymptote in logits per doubling of the word number; is the word number at which the asymptotes intersect; 50 ωSF is the width of the corner in doublings of the word number. The profile of the density is described by the same power curve as in the law of the collapse rate, PF (p) = µP + AF pγF , and the profile of the text share by the straight line QF = λQF + κQF (s 1)/v. All three laws were fitted with weights inverse to the full covariance of the bins, as in Section 4.4. The width of the corner, like the width of the transition of the plateau of the grid, is not determined by the data: its estimate converges to the lower boundary of the search region and is held there, so no noticeable rounding of the corner was found. By the rule of Section 4.4 the shifts of the laws of the word number and the density equal their horizontal asymptotes: µSF = 5.15 1.37 at the beginning of the answer and µP = 3.99 1.53 as 0. The shift of the text share equals the value of the straight line at the beginning of the text: λQF = 0.13 0.64. The contribution of the density is about 0.5 logits at the density 1/512 and about 2.2 logits at the density 1/16 and reaches AF = 7.0 logits at full density: in dense text the model loses the text earlier. The line of the text share passes through the beginning of the textits shift does not differ from zeroand by the end of the text adds κQF to the logit of . The text length and the number of rules do not serve as axes of the place of the collapse. If bins of the text length are added to the model, the test of the hypothesis that they are all zero by the cluster covariance gives Wald statistic of 13.9 with 7 degrees of freedom, = 0.053: beyond the word number and the passed share of the text, the length does not determine the place of the collapse. The bins of the number of rules added to the model differ from zero (p < 0.001), but in one way only: tasks with one rule lose the text earlier than the others at the same word number, density and text share, while the bins from two to 128 rules lie 0.51.9 logits below the bin of one rule with no trend in the number of rules. The profiles of the word number, the density and the text share change by no more than 1.1 of their uncertainty when the bins of the number of rules are added, so the law of the place of the collapse does not depend on this check. The law of the place of the collapse answers the question left by the law of the rate (Section 5.4.1): does the risk of losing the text on the next line grow as the answer progresses or with the volume of the whole text. The place of the loss is determined by the word number and the passed share of the text, while the text length beyond them does not determine it. Consequently, the risk grows as the answer progresses: the further the model has advanced in the answer, the more likely it is that it has already lost the text. Apparently, in long text the collapse is more frequent primarily because the answer to it is longer. 54 The plateau at the beginning of the answer admits an interpretation within the copying mechanism proposed for the collapse rate. At the beginning of the answer the place in the text is set by the very beginning of the input: the first lines of the answer repeat the first lines of the text, and the model has almost nothing to confuse them with. As the answer progresses, the place in the text is held only by the coincidence of the last words of the answer with fragment of the input, and each next line becomes new opportunity to lose this coincidence. The density acts on the place of the collapse in the same direction as on its rate: in dense text there are more replacement words breaking the coincidence of the answer with the input, and the text is lost earlier. The instrument measures the form of the dependence, but not its cause, and the interpretation proposed requires separate test. Thus, for the requests that lost the text, up to the 40th word of the answer the contribution of the word number to the odds that the text is already lost is constant, and after the 40th word these odds grow with the word number; in addition, they grow with the passed share of the text and with the replacement density. The risk of losing the text is determined by the progress through the answer, not by the volume of the text as such.

sections.title: 5.5.1 Instruction capacity
sections.content: Since in the VS-PMR model the rules are represented by two variables, the meaning of the instruction capacity changes as well. The rules of task are described by two axes: the number of rules in the table and the number of the checked rule. An added rule loads the language model twice: the table becomes one line longer, which is accounted for by the axis of the number of rules, and the new line is executed at its place in the list, which is accounted for by the axis of the rule number. Therefore the capacity in the passport is not the number of rules at which the probability of right replacement in an individual trial falls to q, but the number of rules for which the reserve of the level suffices if each rule is paid for along both axes.

sections.title: 5.5.2 Fatigue capacity
sections.content: The fatigue execution capacity (Fatigue Execution Capacity, FEC) FECq is the capacity along the word position in the answer (Section 4.5): the word number at which the loss of the logit due to progress through the answer exhausts the reserve of the level q. This loss is set by the slanted asymptote of the grid law λS + κS log2 (Section 5.3.1). 56 The grid law describes each slice by hyperbolaa smooth transition between two regimes: the plateau and fatigue, that is, the decrease of the logit with the word number. The hyperbolic transition between two straight lines was proposed by Griffiths and Miller, and Ferreira and Zocchi showed that such hyperbola is the expectation of broken line of two straight lines with fixed slopes and intercepts over the distribution of random transition point, namely non-standard t-distribution with two degrees of freedom [8]. In this reading the smoothness of the transition reflects the scatter of the transition point between requests with the straight lines of both regimes common to them, and the law of the fatigue regime is the slanted asymptote. It is one for all slices and does not depend on the volume of the text. The fatigue capacity is counted, like the instruction capacity, from the reference level αphys (Section 5.5.1), and the word number FECq is found from the condition whence αphys + λS + κS log2 FECq = η(q, σ2), log2 FECq = η(q, σ2) αphys λS κS . The uncertainty is computed in the same way as the uncertainty of the instruction capacity. For GPT-4o mini the slope of the asymptote is κS = 2.67 0.31 logits per doubling of the position, and its value at the first word after the shift correction is λS = 17.39 3.37. The reserve of the level 0.95, 0.95 = 13.84 logits, is exhausted at the word FEC0.95 = 3277 571, within the measured region, whose texts extend to 10 240 words. The reserve of the level 0.5, 0.5 = 18.81, is exhausted at the word FEC0.5 = 11 890 1839, beyond the edge of the measured region, and this estimate is obtained by extrapolating the law. The reference level corresponds to the zero point, so the fatigue capacity describes the decrease of the quality of replacements with the word number in the answer without load by replacement rules. Thus GPT-4o mini keeps the share of right replacements at 0.95 over approximately 3300 words of the answer, and at 0.5, by extrapolation of the law, over approximately 12 thousand words.

sections.title: 5.5.3 Guaranteed instruction capacity
sections.content: The guaranteed instruction capacity (Instructional Guaranteed Capacity, IGC) IGCq is the instruction capacity at full replacement density = 1, when every word of the text is replaced; the other axes are taken at the zero point. At = 1 every rule comes with its own word of the text, = m, and as rules are added the density stays equal to one. Therefore the contribution of the density does not depend on the number of rules and enters the cumulative price of the table once, not the price of each rule: CP (m) = fM (m) eR(r) eP (1), where eP (1) is the contribution of the density at = 1 after the shift correction (Section 5.3.2). The capacity is defined by the same condition as the instruction capacity: r= CP (IGCq) = q, = αphys η(q, σ2). The contribution of the density decreases as grows, and at full density the loss is largest, so IGCq serves as lower bound of the instruction capacity over the replacement density. The capacity exists if the reserve of the level is larger than this loss, > eP (1); otherwise the language model does not hold the level already with one rule. 57 By the bins the contribution of the density is the corrected coefficient of the last density bin K, which contains only full density: ePK = θP δP . This bin belongs to the density axis and is common to all requests, so the computation by the bins here, as for the instruction capacity, does not depend on the law. The cumulative price and the capacity by the bins are CP (m) = r=2 a(r) ePK, IGCq = m0 + CP (m0) a(m0 + 1) , m0 = max{ : CP (m) }, where the price of rule a(r) = (r) eR(r), (r) = fMk fMk1 Bk , eR(r) = eRk, Bk, is the same as in Section 5.5.1. For GPT-4o mini the corrected coefficient of the full density bin is ePK = 9.22 1.04, and the (cid:0)1 e1/pc (cid:1) = 9.35 1.01 logits. After deducting the loss from full density, the reserve of the level 0.95 decreases threefold, from 13.84 to 4.6 logits by the bins and 4.5 by the laws, while the capacity decreases only twofold.
